items.title: Long paths in windows
items.text:
During installation on windows one can encounter the following error:

ERROR: Could not install packages due to an OSError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'C:\\Users\\af24\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\pip-install-i3syxwx0\\imgui-bundle_3462a851e1e44f9caa7b8510206f002e\\external\\hello_imgui\\hello_imgui\\hello_imgui_cmake\\android\\apkCMake\\templates\\sdl\\gradle_template\\app\\src\\main\\java\\org\\libsdl\\app\\HIDDeviceBLESteamController.java'
HINT: This error might have occurred since this system does not have Windows Long Path support enabled. You can find information on how to enable this at https://pip.pypa.io/warnings/enable-long-paths

The issues can be fixed by entering Registry Editor and modifying LongPathsEnabled variable under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem from "0" to "1".

Refer to this webpage on the instructions to fix it.

items.title: Cellpose "use GPU" is greyed out (segmentation is very slow)
items.text:
Cellpose (and Suite2p) only offer GPU acceleration when PyTorch exposes a GPU backend — CUDA (NVIDIA) or MPS (Apple Silicon). A CPU-only PyTorch build disables the "use GPU" checkbox. This is common on Windows, where PyPI's default torch wheel is CPU-only.

Check the installed build (in the NeuroSeq environment):

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"

…+cpu / False means CPU-only. If the machine has an NVIDIA (or Apple-Silicon) GPU, install a GPU build and relaunch:

uv pip install --torch-backend=auto torch

Not using uv (e.g. NeuroSeq is installed into a conda environment)? Install directly with pip instead:

pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

If the machine has only Intel integrated graphics, Cellpose cannot use it (CUDA/MPS only) — run segmentation on a GPU machine and import its _seg.npy instead. See Importing imaging data → GPU acceleration for details.

items.title: Examples of brian2 models
items.text: The examples provide a list of brian2 models. The first set of models is tailored to the real neurobiological experiments, and the description of the models contains additional information on the relation of the model architecture and properties with real experiments. The parameters of the models in the examples and initial conditions can be defined and modified in "File -> Edit Model".

items.title: Stimulation protocol
items.text:
In this example, a experimental protocol of electrophysiological and optogenetic interrogation of single neuron is presented. The protocol consists of a current injections, ramps and steps, of varying amplitude and duration:

  • two positive current 100 ms ramps with 300 pA and 600 pA maximum amplitude
  • three 100 ms steps of 200, 400 and 600 pA
  • two ramps (100 ms, 50% and 100% of light power, respectively)
  • three optogenetic stimulation steps for excitatory and inhibitory opsins (25%, 50% and 100% of light power).

items.title: Computational model
items.text:
A single Hodgkin-Huxley neuron is simulated. The model supports direct current injection into the neuron (virtual current clamp) and optogenetic control via a pair of opsins (for excitation and inhibition). The injected current into the neuron can be controlled via I_external stimulation array that supports both positive and negative current values with units expressed in pA. The neuron is complemented by two additional conductances that can be modulated by light that represent optogenetic tools (opsins). As no intrinsic kinetics of opsins is taken into account, the opsins are considered to be ideal and have an immediate activation and deactivation. Exc_stimulation and Inh_stimulation are corresponding arrays with units being a fraction of predefined maximum conductances of opsin.

The number of neurons in the model can be increased and stim array will be updated accordingly . As there is no synaptic connections between them, they will operate independently.

Reversal potentials and conductances defined in the model:

\[E_{rev}^{exc} = 0 mV\] \[E_{rev}^{inh} = - 80 mV\] \[g_{exc} = 0.1 \ mS \ cm^{-2}\] \[g_{inh} = 0.1 \ mS \ cm^{-2}\]

No other external inputs (e.g. gausian noise) was implemented in the model. The model can be configured for non-neuronal cell by setting up conductances for \(Na\) and \(K\) voltage gated channels to zero.

items.title: Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire Neuron

items.title: Network of Hodgkin-Huxley Neurons

items.title: Analysis Plugins (Developer)
items.text: This page describes how the custom analysis plugin system works internally and how to implement new analysis plugins.

items.title: Architecture Overview
items.text:
Plugin support is split across three core modules:

  • src/neuroseq/analysis_plugins.py
  • Discovers plugin modules from src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins and from the per-user folder returned by user_plugins_directory() (user plugins never shadow built-in filenames or PLUGIN_IDs)
  • Loads each plugin file dynamically
  • Builds AnalysisPlugin objects (id, label, icon, render)
  • src/neuroseq/visualization/timeseries_widget.py
  • Rebuilds right-click analysis menu on demand
  • Adds built-in analysis actions and plugin actions
  • Emits custom_analysis_requested with either a built-in CustomAnalysisType or an AnalysisPlugin
  • src/neuroseq/visualization/custom_analysis_widget.py
  • Executes built-in analysis logic
  • Executes plugin render callback for plugin analyses
  • Catches plugin exceptions, logs the plugin id, and shows a failure message in the plot

items.title: Plugin Discovery
items.text:
A plugin is a Python file in: src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins. It must have *.py extention (files starting with _ will be ignored) and define callable render_analysis. Each pluging has ID, NAME and ICON. The default value for ID and NAME is a filename without extention but user can also define them as PLUGIN_ID, PLUGIN_NAME, and PLUGIN_ICON (e.g. mdi6.puzzle). PLUGIN_ID should be stable over time. Use a machine-oriented id (for example, mean_activity) and keep display text in PLUGIN_NAME. At the present momement dropdown menu does not distinguish the type of the data that is being analysed and shows all improrted plugins regardless of datatype.

See src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins/mean_activity.py for a working example plugin.

items.title: Advanced Interactive Example
items.text:
The ELiSe plugins are thin wrappers; their supporting code is a regular package, src/neuroseq/elise_support/: replay_metrics.py provides replay metrics and CSV export, workflows.py connects project data to the analysis windows, and protocol_dialog.py provides protocol settings. Keep core code out of the plugin folder: it is scanned and executed on every right-click menu and is excluded from coverage.

For an advanced plugin example with UI controls, see src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins/advanced_mean_activity.py.

This plugin extends the basic mean-activity analysis by adding an interactive control bar in the same analysis window.

important: for the analysis widgets opened in the same window as it is the case for "show custom analysis" pad it is important to prevent duplicating of controls when the same plugin is run repeatedly in one open analysis widget.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: The NeuroSeq is an open-source project. Everyone can suggest and implement improvements as well as improve overall reliability and stability of its operation.

items.title: Development pipeline
items.text:
1. Fork and clone repository.
  2. Create a feature branch.
  3. Install in editable mode.
  4. Modify the code.
  5. Test new functionality.
  6. Run pytests before opening a pull request.

items.title: Project workspaces
items.text:
gui.py contains the application shell. Each tab embeds a separate ProjectWorkspace from project_workspace.py, which owns its project's widgets, controllers, console namespace, undo history, input designers, detached windows, and background jobs. The workspace uses a child QMainWindow to lay out its own menus and toolbars. Gui.active_workspace is the explicit access point for the current tab; Gui.project and forwarded attribute reads remain available for integrations.

Switching tabs changes the visible workspace without calling update_project() or copying widget state into Project. Playback pauses when leaving a tab; background jobs continue and deliver their results to their owning workspace. update_project() refreshes data within a workspace, for example after imports or model edits. GUI state remains in memory and is not serialized to .nseq.

Settings and physical connections are application resources. workspace_devices.py shares the ScanImage connection and SysCon2 transport. Each SysCon2 panel receives a session that routes command replies to the requesting workspace; connection status is shared. Only the active workspace receives live ScanImage frames. Acquisition results are matched by run ID to the workspace that requested them. Closing a tab stops its jobs and releases its resources without disconnecting other tabs. Application shutdown checks unsaved projects individually and stops all workspaces before shutting down the shared connections.

Run uv run pytest tests/test_project_workspaces.py for tab isolation, background result routing, device sessions, and workspace lifecycle tests. Existing widget and workflow tests exercise ProjectWorkspace directly.

items.title: Integration of Custom Simulators
items.text: This page describes the current structure used for NeuroSeq external simulators and how to implement a new backend.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
NeuroSeq has built-in Brian2 simulator but also supports arbitraty simulation backends. These backends are loaded through Project.load_external_simulator() and are expected to produce an Experiment object from stimulus arrays.

There are now two layers:

  1. A shared base class in src/neuroseq/example_models/NN.py.
  2. A backend implementation class such as src/neuroseq/example_models/elise.py.

The base class is intentionally lightweight. It does not use abc; instead, subclass methods are expected to override the base methods and the defaults raise NotImplementedError.

items.title: Structure of the Base NN Class
items.text:
The shared NN class in src/neuroseq/example_models/NN.py provides common state and parameter handling.

It currently contains:

  1. __init__(default_params_schema) Stores a deep copy of the editable parameter schema, initializes flat parameter values from the schema defaults, and initializes cumulative simulated time.
  2. simulated_time_seconds Property exposing the amount of simulated time already accumulated by the backend instance.
  3. default_params_schema() Returns a deep copy of the editable parameter schema for use in the GUI.
  4. flat_default_params() Returns a flat {name: default_value} mapping derived from the schema.
  5. update_params(params) Merges user-provided parameter overrides onto defaults and resets backend state if anything changed.
  6. _flat_defaults() Internal helper that flattens the schema into default values.
  7. reset() Subclass hook that must clear backend-specific runtime state.
  8. simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=None) Subclass hook that must run one simulation chunk and return an Experiment.

The important design point is that the base class owns parameter bookkeeping and cumulative time, while the subclass owns backend-specific runtime objects.

items.title: Structure of a Backend Implementation
items.text:
An implementation module should define a backend class derived from NN. The ELISE backend in src/neuroseq/example_models/elise.py is the current reference implementation.

The backend class should typically provide:

  1. __init__() Calls super().__init__(DEFAULT_PARAMS) and initializes backend-specific runtime fields such as cached networks, signatures, RNG state, or imported backend types.
  2. reset() Clears runtime state that should be rebuilt when parameters change.
  3. Backend-specific initialization helpers For example, ELISE uses _import_elise_types() and _initialize_network(num_vis).
  4. simulate(...) Validates inputs, applies parameter updates, initializes or reuses the backend state, advances the simulation, and returns an Experiment containing the generated data.

For stateful backends, simulate(...) should preserve runtime state between calls so repeated runs can continue from the previous state instead of starting over.

items.title: Module-Level Entry Points
items.text:
For integration with the current project and GUI code, the module should expose these entry points:

  1. simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=None) Compatibility wrapper used by the existing call sites.
  2. get_simulator() Returns the singleton backend instance.
  3. NN Constructor used by Project.load_external_simulator() when a module exposes a class-based backend entry point.
  4. A singleton instance such as _SIMULATOR = Elise().

This keeps the current GUI and project logic simple while still allowing a class-based implementation internally.

When restoring an archive, Project calls the backend instance's optional migrate_project(project) method after loading the simulator and project data. Backends can use this hook to upgrade their own legacy stimulus formats. The ELISE implementation keeps these conversions, its example project factory (create_project()), and teaching-pattern helpers in src/neuroseq/example_models/elise.py. The example menu registers a small wrapper in example_projects/networks/elise_project.py that delegates to this factory.

Example project factories live in src/neuroseq/example_projects/, with one project per file under neurons/ or networks/. The package's __init__.py exports the factories and imports them in their existing menu order. _registry.py provides the register_example_project decorator. New examples should define a decorated factory in the appropriate folder, import it in the package entry point, and add it to __all__ so it is exported and appears in the example-project menu.

items.title: Expected Data Flow
items.text:
The external simulator call path is:

  1. The GUI collects stimulus arrays into stims_dict.
  2. Project.load_external_simulator() loads either: a. a built-in NeuroSeq simulator module such as neuroseq:elise, or b. a Python file containing a simulate(...) entry point.
  3. The backend simulate(...) method returns an Experiment.
  4. The GUI offers the returned experiment for import or append into the project.

items.title: Minimal Template
items.text:
from collections.abc import Mapping

from neuroseq.data import Experiment
from neuroseq.example_models.NN import ParamValue
from neuroseq.example_models.NN import NN

DEFAULT_PARAMS = {
    "example_param": {
        "value": 1.0,
        "default": 1.0,
        "type": "float",
        "group": "General",
        "description": "Example parameter.",
    }
}


class MyBackend(NN):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(DEFAULT_PARAMS)
        self._runtime = None

    def reset(self) -> None:
        self._runtime = None
        self._simulated_time_s = 0.0

    def simulate(
        self,
        stims_dict: dict,
        simulation_time: float,
        params: Mapping[str, ParamValue] | None = None,
    ) -> Experiment:
        self.update_params(params)
        # build or reuse runtime state
        # run the backend
        # return Experiment(...)
        raise NotImplementedError


def simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=None):
    return _SIMULATOR.simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=params)


def get_simulator() -> MyBackend:
    return _SIMULATOR


_SIMULATOR = MyBackend()

items.title: Notes
items.text:
1. The GUI parameter editor consumes the schema stored in project.external_simulate_params, so schema keys and value types should remain simple.
  2. The Experiment returned by the backend should be self-contained for the run chunk that was just simulated.
  3. If the backend is stateful, use self._simulated_time_s to align repeated runs with previously simulated time.

items.title: Developer Guide on installation and use
items.text: Choose either uv or a direct Conda installation. uv can manage Python and the project .venv independently, so it does not require Conda. The two workflows are alternatives; you do not need to set up both.

items.title: Developer Installation with uv
items.text:
First ensure you have installed uv.

Then you can install prek (a faster implementation of pre-commit) using uv:

uv tool install prek

Then clone the repository and set up the pre-commit hooks for this repository:

git clone git@github.com:neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq
uv sync --group dev
prek install

The documentation is in the docs folder as Markdown and rendered using Zensical. To serve the documentation locally run:

uv run zensical serve

Open the URL shown in the terminal to see the generated documentation. See Documentation for build checks and deployment details.

items.title: Developer Installation without uv
items.text:
Alternatively, if you aren't using uv, then create a new conda environment or virtual environment and activate it. Then do an editable install of the package (which means that any changes to the source code will be reflected in the installed package without needing to reinstall), and install the pre-commit hooks:

conda create -n neuroseq python=3.12
conda activate neuroseq
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -e . --group dev
python -m pip install prek
prek install

The --group dev option requires a recent pip. This installs directly into Conda and does not reproduce uv.lock or uv's package-index configuration. If you install uv inside Conda and then use uv sync / uv run, the project uses its separate .venv by default. See installation and environment selection.

items.title: Developer Use
items.text:
The GUI is launched with:

uv run neuroseq

(if you are not using uv, just run neuroseq)

To run with profiling:

uv run neuroseq --profile --profile-output latest.prof

and to see the results:

 uv run snakeviz latest.prof

To run the test suite:

uv run pytest

For the direct Conda installation, use python -m pytest in the activated environment, or conda run -n neuroseq python -m pytest. Run application and tests with the same interpreter when investigating dependency failures.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: This project uses Zensical, configured in zensical.toml at the repository root. The published documentation is at https://neuroseq.github.io/.

items.title: To run docs locally
items.text:
For the uv workflow, install the development dependencies, which include Zensical:

uv sync --locked

Start the local documentation server from the repository root:

uv run zensical serve

Then open the local URL shown in the terminal.

If NeuroSeq is installed directly into Conda, activate that environment, install the documentation packages with python -m pip install --group docs, and run zensical serve instead. See environment selection.

items.title: Optional: build static docs
items.text:
To generate static files for deployment:

uv run zensical build --clean --strict

The generated site is written to the site/ folder.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: The docs GitHub Actions workflow runs the same clean, strict build on all pull requests and pushes to the main branch. Only pushes to main publish the generated site to the main branch of neuroseq/neuroseq.github.io. It can also be run manually on main using Run workflow.

items.title: Why not publish directly?
items.text:
The reason to push to and publish from neuroseq/neuroseq.github.io is so that the published site is located at https://neuroseq.github.io/, i.e. org-name.github.io.

If it was published directly from this repo, the url would be https://neuroseq.github.io/neuroseq, i.e. org-name.github.io/repo-name - but if in the future you get a custom domain name for neuroseq then the extra repo, deploy key etc would no longer be needed and the neuroseq.github.io repo could be removed.

items.title: Project data undo and redo
items.text:
src/neuroseq/project_history.py contains the Qt-independent ProjectHistory and ProjectCommand classes. Each Project owns a history; stimulation modifiers use that same instance. Edits across input arrays and experimental data are undone in chronological order, regardless of the selected input.

The shared history records stimulation value edits, generated patterns, padding and trimming, and experimental-data additions, appends, replacements and deletions. Deleting several data groups is one command. Appending retains the previous arrays and timing metadata, including data overwritten by overlapping time ranges. A failed append restores all affected datasets without recording a command. Redo uses the retained data and does not repeat file import.

Commands provide a label and redo() / undo() callbacks. Use history.execute(command) to apply a new command, or history.record_applied(command) after a successful mutation. Callbacks should validate before mutation or roll back partial failures. Commands must operate on project data without retaining Qt widgets. History listeners refresh the views; bound-method listeners are weak and observers can explicitly unsubscribe.

Experiment mutators retain array buffers by reference and copy metadata, rather than copying a whole project or its simulator. These mutators replace buffers when changing data; writing into retained buffers in place would invalidate a snapshot. Direct console mutations do not automatically create commands.

Refreshing an existing workspace preserves history. Histories belong to each project independently, remain available after saving, and are not serialized in .nseq archives. Loaded projects start with an empty history. Undo and redo mark the project dirty, even when undo happens to return to its last saved content.

Existing non-undoable input restructuring operations (creation, renaming, deletion, resampling, neuron remapping and looping) clear the history because older commands can reference obsolete names or sample indices. Importing project components also starts a new baseline. Simulator checkpoints, device state and hardware activity remain outside this history. Workspace undo and redo are disabled while a background operation is running.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
A proper development of the code implies the use of tests with the pytest framework. Tests are located in the tests/ folder.

Use the same environment that runs the application. For a uv checkout, install the development dependencies with uv sync --group dev and use uv run below. An activated Conda environment does not make these commands use Conda's Python; uv uses the project's .venv by default.

For an installation directly into Conda, replace uv run pytest with conda run -n neuroseq python -m pytest (or python -m pytest after activation). See environment selection.

items.title: To run all tests
items.text: uv run pytest

items.title: To run a specific subset of tests
items.text: uv run pytest tests/test_gui.py

items.title: SysCon2 control
items.text:
The protocol, connection manager, panel, and routine tests use fake transports and recordings. On Windows, tests/test_syscon2_client.py also opens a real local named pipe to check timeouts when a server never replies or drains a write. These tests do not require SysCon2 or a connected stimulation device.

uv run pytest tests/test_syscon2_client.py tests/test_syscon2_connection_manager.py tests/test_syscon2_panel.py tests/test_rheobase_dialog.py tests/test_stdp_window_dialog.py

Real-rig checks are still needed for command execution and acquisition alignment. The SCI v1.2 manual confirms the Sequence Manager instance name for the Holo4D profile and that Runs = 0 means endless repetition, but does not specify the wire width of the Runs integer. The client currently uses a 32-bit DWord.

Pipe commands have a 30-second deadline, configurable through NamedPipeTransport(timeout=...). Disconnect and shutdown cancel pending I/O. A timeout closes the connection and requires an explicit reconnect; it does not confirm that a queued Stop command reached the device.

items.title: Real-rig checklist
items.text:
This updates the export/control test and rheobase test in the PR. Those comments describe the overall workflow correctly, but the following details matter when testing the current implementation.

  1. Run NeuroSeq and SysCon2 on the same Windows PC, with the Holo4D profile and a verified Cellpose-to-stim-ID mapping. Connect opens the pipe; it does not prove the laser is connected or ready. Click Get Status to discover lightsources and retrieve status; the selector prefers 940 nm. Check the mode and hardware state in SysCon2. Direct laser mutation controls are hidden.
  2. Prepare a short pattern and use Export with settings…. Select the intended input array, wavelength, target power, LUT, and output directory. The export target power is in mW. LUT percentages are divided by 100 in .seq files; verify this scaling on the rig. Live status uses the unit configured in SysCon2, which SCI does not identify.
  3. Run Check Input Sanity and resolve every reported violation. The exact required timestep is 520.8125 µs (0.0005208125 seconds), not exactly 520.8 µs. Let the dialog resample it. Around 20 ms is a starting pulse duration, but it does not by itself guarantee valid SLM timing; inspect the generated overview and debug CSV after the sanity fixes.
  4. Generate the script. Filenames use the dialog's Script name, whose initial value follows export_seq_<date>_<n>, rather than the array name. The PNG is a generated preview. The panel shows whether import is pending, confirmed, failed, or not attempted (offline). Red target crosses appear only after acknowledgement of that preview's import and exclude skipped neurons. They do not show remote selection, upload, or live illumination. Confirm the sequence also appears in SysCon2 itself before proceeding.
  5. Select the imported sequence, set Runs = 1, choose the start condition and trigger edge, then click Upload, wait for "Press Run", then click Run and confirm. Verify the progress label moves through uploading, hardware readiness, starting, and running. A triggered run must wait for its trigger. Stop during upload must not send Run afterward. SCI reports phases rather than percentage completion. Validate actual timing, pattern, and delivered power using the rig's controlled bench-test procedure. Configure emission, shutter, and laser intensity in SysCon2 itself.
  6. Edit the array and test Export current array to stimulation setup. It reuses the last dialog export's settings but writes export_seq_<date>_<n>.seq and its diagnostic files to a temporary directory, not the dialog's chosen output folder. The Target power box beside it overrides only the power. It opens the full export dialog if settings are unavailable. As above, verify the import, then select and use Upload then Run for the changed sequence.
  7. For rheobase, select the SysCon2 target and use amplitudes within 0–1. Set power, laser and spots under Hardware settings; they are the project's export settings, so no prior Export with settings… is needed. Choose the post-pulse window from the actual acquisition frame rate: at 30 Hz, 100–300 ms spans several frames; neither 30 Hz nor a particular useful response window is guaranteed by the SCI protocol.
  8. Automatic blocks (default): connect ScanImage in the ScanImage (imaging) tab, set its recording folder, and load a Cellpose segmentation of the field of view. Wire the sequence's TTL output (the configuration's TargetConnectorPort) to ScanImage's acquisition trigger. Start the routine: for every block NeuroSeq imports, selects and uploads it, arms a triggered recording (block plus Record after block), runs it and extracts ΔF/F. The routine log names the run's folder; check that every block's .seq, overview and sidecar are kept there and that each recording's .json names the right .seq. Verify the recording starts with the block (sequence start to first frame), that each <date>_<number>.tif holds the requested frames, and that the logged ΔF/F rise (ΔF/F readout) or deconvolved spike count (spike readout) matches the cell's visible response. Tune the spike threshold on a few probes first: OASIS event sizes are in ΔF/F, so it depends on expression level.
  9. Manual blocks (automatic unticked): for every block, refresh the sequence list, select the newly imported block, set Runs = 1, then Upload, Run and acquire. The host only imports. Import each probe into a new experiment with a unique name, starting at time zero for that block, and return to the routine to click Calcium data imported. Fresh-data selection is resolved when that button is clicked, and existing recordings are rejected, including on the first probe. For raw TIFF import, use the Suite2p option if you measure deconvolved spikes.
  10. Check pause, stale-data rejection, and stopping. Routine Stop ends the software search and cancels only its own block: a running sequence gets a Stop command and an armed recording is aborted, but a block whose import is already queued still completes on the hardware. Use Holo4D Stop and verify the hardware state on the rig. If communication stalls, a queued Stop cannot be assumed delivered; Disconnect cancels communication, not stimulation.

Record the script/debug CSV, selected sequence, Runs, trigger settings, wavelength, power settings, actual frame rate, import threshold, and per-probe response. Confirm the Runs wire representation on the real system; the Sequence Manager instance name is documented in the manual and is no longer an unresolved naming assumption. The same per-block rules apply to the STDP target; pairing blocks need no recording (automatic pairings are run without one; manual ones need acknowledgement after execution).

items.title: Linux teardown crash with Conda
items.text:
If tests report success and then segfault during process exit, inspect the native backtrace. On the development host, this occurred in Conda's libstdc++ exit handlers after graphics libraries unloaded. Running with the system C++ runtime resolved the crash without changing application code:

conda run --no-capture-output -n neuroseq env LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6 QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen QT_API=pyqt6 PYTEST_QT_API=pyqt6 .venv/bin/python -m pytest

The library path is specific to Debian/Ubuntu x86-64; check the system library location before using this workaround elsewhere.

items.title: Pre-commit
items.text:
pre-commit run --all-files

Export validation is shared by the dialog, quick export, and routine host. Timing fixes must first be reviewed and applied with Check Input Sanity. Other warnings (including skipped neurons, missing power calibration, and power clamping) require confirmation before a dialog or quick export can proceed; unattended routine exports reject these warnings. Existing dialog export files require overwrite confirmation. An import uses a private snapshot, so regenerating the same filename cannot change an already queued request. Disconnecting or changing projects clears preview import confirmation and target markers. Importing an arbitrary file clears the generated preview association because its targets are unknown.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
NeuroSeq requires Python 3.12 or newer. Choose one of the following workflows and use the same environment for launching, testing, and troubleshooting.

Option Environment Requires Conda? Launch command uv Project .venv, managed by uv No uv run neuroseq Conda with pip Named Conda environment Yes neuroseq after activation

items.title: Option 1: Repository installation with uv
items.text:
uv works independently of Conda and can download a suitable Python interpreter when needed. You do not need to create or activate a Conda environment for this option.

Install uv, then run:

git clone git@github.com:neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq
uv sync
uv run neuroseq

GitHub SSH access is required for this clone URL. uv sync creates a project environment in .venv and installs dependencies using pyproject.toml and uv.lock. uv run checks that environment before launching a command. No manual activation of .venv is needed. See uv's project workflow.

After pulling repository updates, run uv sync again. To deliberately resolve newer dependency versions, use uv lock --upgrade followed by uv sync and test the result; this changes uv.lock.

items.title: Option 2: Conda
items.text:
Conda is an alternative to the project .venv. Install Anaconda if needed.

Once Anaconda installed, create and activate a new environment in a command line:

conda create -n neuroseq python=3.12
conda activate neuroseq

Alternatively, the new enviroment can be created within Anaconda Navigator. For this, open Anaconda Navigator and go to "Enviroments". Click "Create" button, write "neuroseq" as a name and select Python 3.12.

items.title: Install NeuroSeq into Conda
items.text:
NeuroSeq requires Python 3.12 or newer.

If you have ssh authentication to GitHub set up you can install directly from this repository with pip:

pip install git+ssh://git@github.com/neuroseq/neuroseq

Alternatively you can clone the repository and then install it:

git clone git@github.com:neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq
pip install .

Run neuroseq from the activated Conda environment. Prefer python -m pip install . to explicitly install into its Python. To update the installation after pulling changes, run python -m pip install --upgrade .. Use python -m pip check to check dependency metadata.

Pip does not use uv.lock or [tool.uv.sources], so this installation can have different package versions and PyTorch builds from the uv workflow. For GPU setup, see GPU troubleshooting.

items.title: Using uv from a Conda shell
items.text:
Combining uv and Conda is optional, not a third required setup step. You may install uv in an activated Conda environment:

conda activate neuroseq
python -m pip install uv
uv sync
uv run neuroseq

With the default project configuration, uv run uses the repository's .venv, even when Conda is active. Conda supplies the shell/tool installation; the application dependencies remain in the separate uv environment. In particular, conda run -n neuroseq python and uv run python can load different packages. Updating one does not repair or update the other.

For a fully independent uv setup, install standalone uv using the link above and run it from a shell without Conda activated. If your current uv executable is installed inside Conda, install standalone uv before removing that Conda environment. An existing project .venv may also use a Conda-provided Python; when retiring that Python installation, recreate .venv with a uv-managed Python interpreter.

To identify the environment and Brian2/NumPy versions actually used, run:

uv run python -c "import sys, brian2, numpy; print(sys.executable); print(brian2.__version__, numpy.__version__)"

For a direct Conda installation, run the same check with conda run -n neuroseq python -c "import sys, brian2, numpy; print(sys.executable); print(brian2.__version__, numpy.__version__)". In the application's embedded console, import sys; print(sys.executable) identifies the running interpreter. Point your IDE at that same interpreter.

items.title: Windows desktop shortcut
items.text: On Windows, NeuroSeq can instead be installed with a desktop shortcut that updates it from GitHub before each start. See Windows desktop shortcut.

items.title: How to install Cython on Windows
items.text:
To speed up simulations with cython on Windows one will need an installation of the Microsoft Visual C++ 14.0 or higher.

See this stackoverflow post for further instructions on installation:

Visual Studio 2022 is available here

items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
After installing, you should be able to run the following command to launch the GUI:

neuroseq

The GUI contains many buttons and widgets, the meaning of which will be clarified in the next sections. Once the NeuroSeq GUI is opened, try to quickly run a default simulation example by clicking "Simulate -> Run simulaiton" (shortcut: Ctrl + R). You will be then asked about the prefered duration of simulation (default is 1.0). Click ok and wait once the simulation is completed.

Let's use this example to give an overview of GUI and its functionality, described in GUI Overview section.

items.title: Windows desktop shortcut
items.text: On Windows, NeuroSeq can be started from a desktop shortcut that first updates it from main on GitHub. NeuroSeq then runs from a git clone with uv, so the installed version always matches the code, and nobody has to open a prompt to start or update it.

items.title: 1. Install Git and uv
items.text:
• Git: install Git for Windows with the default options.
  • uv: in PowerShell, run the standalone installer:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

If you already use conda, pip install uv inside a conda environment works as well.

Open a new prompt afterwards and check that both work:

git --version
uv --version

items.title: 2. Get NeuroSeq
items.text:
Clone the repository, for example into Documents\GitHub:

cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
mkdir GitHub
cd GitHub
git clone https://github.com/neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq

The HTTPS address needs no GitHub login, so the shortcut can update without asking for a password.

items.title: 3. Create the shortcut
items.text:
In the same prompt, inside the clone, run:

powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\install_shortcut.ps1

It creates NeuroSeq on the desktop and prints the clone and the uv it will use. If uv came from a conda environment, run this from the Anaconda Prompt with that environment active, because the shortcut remembers that uv.

The script also removes an older desktop shortcut that starts a pip-installed neuroseq.exe, since that copy does not follow the clone. Pass -KeepOld to keep it. Run the script again after moving the clone or uv.

items.title: 4. First start
items.text:
The first install downloads all dependencies, including PyTorch with CUDA support (several GB), which can take many minutes. Run it once in the same prompt so you can follow its progress:

uv sync

Then double-click NeuroSeq. Later starts are quick, unless an update changed the dependencies; the shortcut shows no progress while it installs them, so give it time instead of starting it again.

items.title: What the shortcut does
items.text:
Each time it starts NeuroSeq, the shortcut:

  1. Updates the clone from GitHub. This only happens when the clone is on main, has no changes to tracked files, and the update is a fast-forward. Untracked files, such as data, do not prevent it.
  2. Starts NeuroSeq with uv run, which first brings the clone's .venv in line with uv.lock. This takes longer than usual only after an update changed the dependencies.

If the update cannot run, NeuroSeq still starts with the current version, and a notice that closes by itself says why. The reasons are: the clone is on another branch, it has local changes, GitHub could not be reached, or the local main has commits that are not on GitHub.

A clone on a feature branch is never moved to main automatically. Switch it back yourself once that work is merged:

git switch main

items.title: Logs
items.text:
Output of the last start is in %LOCALAPPDATA%\neuroseq:

  • launcher.log: the update steps and the commit that was started.
  • neuroseq.out.log and neuroseq.err.log: NeuroSeq's own output. If NeuroSeq stops with an error, the end of neuroseq.err.log is also shown in a message.

To start without updating, for example during an experiment, run:

powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\launch_neuroseq.ps1 -NoUpdate

items.title: Analysis Tools and Custom Plugins
items.text: NeuroSeq provides built-in custom analysis tools to support major types of analysis of neuronal data. It also supports user-defined analysis plugins.

items.title: Use Built-In Analysis Tools
items.text:
1. Generate trace or spike data in a simulation or real experiments.
  2. In corresponding widget, drag to select a neuron/time region.
  3. Right-click the selected area.
  4. Choose one of the built-in analysis actions:
  5. Optionally pick the (new window) variant to open results in a separate window.

items.title: The Custom Analysis widget
items.text:
When an analysis is run without the (new window) variant, its output lands in the Custom analysis dock widget. Toggle it from View → Show Custom analysis in the menu or via the toolbar.

The widget reuses the standard pan/zoom interaction of the other timeseries panels, so you can drag-select inside the analysis output itself and run a follow-up analysis on it.

items.title: ELiSe replay analysis
items.text:
Projects loaded from the ELiSe Sequence Learning Network example get an extra one-click action on the stim editor toolbar: Analyse ELiSe replay (target MSE).

It compares the simulated firing_rate_r trace against the binary teaching pattern derived from the project's opsin_exc stim, computing the paper-style replay MSE and correlation. The button is enabled only when the project is the ELiSe one and a simulation has produced the required trace. Results are appended as a new analysis output and a metrics .csv file is written alongside.

items.title: Use Installed Analysis Plugins
items.text:
NeuroSeq discovers plugins from this folder:

src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins

Any *.py file in that folder is treated as a plugin module (except files starting with _).

NeuroSeq also discovers plugins from a per-user folder outside the package (<user data dir>/neuroseq/analysis_plugins, e.g. ~/.local/share/neuroseq/analysis_plugins on Linux, or the folder named by the NEUROSEQ_USER_PLUGIN_DIR environment variable). Plugins written by the chat assistant go there, and only after you confirm them in a Save plugin dialog (see Chat assistant). A user plugin whose filename or PLUGIN_ID matches a built-in plugin is skipped with a warning.

Plugins can be added and tested during the operation of NeuroSeq: no restarts are necessary.

After placing or editing a plugin file, open the right-click analysis menu again: you should see the plugin of interest in the menu.

items.title: Create Your Own Plugin
items.text:
Users can create a new plugins in src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins, for example:

src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins/my_analysis.py

Each plugin should define:

  • PLUGIN_ID: a short stable internal identifier used in error logging
  • PLUGIN_NAME: a label that will be shown in the context menu
  • PLUGIN_ICON: optional QtAwesome icon name (for example mdi6.chart-line)
  • render_analysis(widget, data, neuron_slice, time_slice): plotting function

For more technical implementation details, see the Developer Guide: Analysis plugins.

items.title: Deliver stimuli to BrainScaleS-2
items.text:
The Stimulation setup pane (View → Show Stimulation setup) has one tab per stimulus-delivery target. Next to SysCon2 (HOLO4D), which drives the holographic stimulation rig, the BrainScaleS-2 tab delivers the current stim array to the BrainScaleS-2 (BSS-2) accelerated neuromorphic chip and adds the chip's response to the project as a new data group.

!!! note "Verified on hardware"

Connection and constant-current delivery work on the real system (chip
`hxcube7fpga0chip57_1` through `quiggeldy.bioai.eu:11750`, October 2026):
a 10-neuron staircase made every neuron fire only during its own pulse,
with the membrane of the recorded neuron read back over the whole run.
See [Results on the chip](#results-on-the-chip).

items.title: How it works
items.text:
NeuroSeq does not import the BSS-2 software stack (pynn_brainscales, dlens_vx_v3); it only exists inside the EBRAINS container image. On Connect, NeuroSeq starts a small helper script inside the container:

singularity exec --bind <neuroseq>/resources/bss2 [--app <app>] <image> \
  bash -c '{ export SYSTEMNAME="ebrainslab";
             source /esd/vendor/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh;
             spack env activate esd; } 1>&2 && exec python -u neuroseq_bss2_helper.py'

NeuroSeq and the helper exchange JSON lines over stdin/stdout. The helper opens a connection to the chip through quiggeldy (the BSS-2 job server) and runs the network with pynn_brainscales. The connection is shared by all open project tabs, but each tab only receives the results of its own runs.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
1. Get the container image. On lab machines the image is /containers/stable/latest (use the app name dls). Elsewhere, download the EBRAINS image, for example:
mkdir -p tmp
SINGULARITY_TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp singularity pull \
  docker://docker-registry.ebrains.eu/esd/master/image:lab_latest.oci

and choose the resulting .sif file with Browse… (leave Container app empty for such an image unless it defines apps).

  1. Choose a setup. The picker always lists the quiggeldy instances on quiggeldy.bioai.eu, which run different software versions: 11717 (stable), 11750 (experimental) and 11780 (special). They are reachable only from allow-listed addresses; ask the BSS-2 team to add your computer's IP. With the EBRAINS lab_latest image only the experimental instance accepted the connection (October 2026); it is the default. The others fail with Could not submit request. Refresh keeps the selected instance when it is still listed. Refresh additionally downloads the EBRAINS setup list (https://quiggeldy.bioai.eu/nmpi/quiggeldy_setups.csv, columns Host,Port,Identifier); its default entry is the one the EBRAINS examples pick: sha256(user name) mod number of setups, where the user name is $USER. Host, port and expected identifier stay editable.

  2. Token (optional). From an allow-listed IP, the quiggeldy instances accept the connection with your user name alone; leave Token empty. For token-based access (e.g. through EBRAINS), paste the output of clb_oauth.get_token() (EBRAINS Lab) into Token. If the field is empty, an existing QUIGGELDY_TOKEN environment variable is used. The token is kept in memory for this session only: it is passed to the container through the helper's environment (QUIGGELDY_TOKEN, also with the SINGULARITYENV_ and APPTAINERENV_ prefixes), never on the command line, and it is not saved in the settings or written to the log. Anything that looks like the token in helper output is masked.

  3. Connect. The first activation of the container's software environment takes around 50 seconds; later connections start in under a second (see Start-up time). The status line reports each step. Once quiggeldy answers, Connected chip shows the chip identifier. If it differs from the selected setup's identifier, the status says so.

The tab settings (image, app, setup, input mode and its parameters, recorded neuron, speed-up) are saved for next time; the token is not.

items.title: Input modes
items.text: Neurons sets how many hardware neurons are driven; auto uses one neuron per stim channel. Stim channel i drives hardware neuron i. Extra channels are dropped and missing ones receive no input, both with a warning. A single-channel stim array drives every neuron. Max neurons (default 512, one chip) caps the count.

items.title: Constant current (stim array) — default
items.text:
The stim array is split into segments wherever any channel's value changes; runs of identical samples form one segment. For each segment and neuron the helper sets

  • constant_current_enable = value > 0, and
  • constant_current_i_offset = round(clip(value / value_at_max, 0, 1) * max_i_offset)

and runs the segment as its own hardware run (pynn.reset() before every segment but the first, then pynn.run(duration)), reading spikes and membrane voltage right after it and shifting them to the segment's start time. Each segment therefore starts from the neurons' resting state. (Chaining segments with RunCommand.APPEND, as in the AdEx tutorial, executed and recorded only the first chained part on the chip.) Max i_offset is in hardware units (0–1022); Stim value at max defaults to the array maximum. Segments that become identical after rounding are merged. Every segment costs about 0.5 s of hardware time (20 segments ≈ 12 s); very many segments (more than 1000) are allowed but slow, so the confirmation warns about them.

items.title: Spike input
items.text:
Spike trains are fed through a SpikeSourceArray population, one source per hardware neuron, with one-to-one excitatory projections of the chosen Weight (0–63). The spike source is either

  • From stim array: the stim array is sampled every Event interval (biological ms); a spike is emitted wherever a channel exceeds Threshold, as in the PyNN example model, or
  • From project spike data: a spike dataset from a data group of the project; neuron i's spikes drive hardware neuron i.

items.title: Time base (speed-up)
items.text:
BSS-2 runs about 1000 times faster than biological neurons, and pynn_brainscales run durations and recorded times are in hardware milliseconds. NeuroSeq works in biological seconds and converts with the Speed-up factor (default 1000):

  • hardware ms = biological s × 1000 / speed-up — 1 s of stimulus is a 1 ms run;
  • biological s = hardware ms / 1000 × speed-up — a spike at 0.5 ms on the chip is stored at 0.5 s.

items.title: Delivery and readback
items.text:
Deliver current stim array shows a summary (neurons, segments or spikes, biological and hardware duration, recorded neuron) and asks for confirmation. While the run executes, the status line shows the helper's progress. The neurons are HXNeurons configured from the chip's nightly calibration (as in the BrainScaleS-2 demos), which the helper loads once per connection with pynn.helper.chip_from_nightly(), falling back to the EBRAINS calibration download for the connected chip. A running BSS-2 run keeps the project tab from closing.

When the run finishes, a data group named BSS-2 <stim name> <date time> is added (undoable with Edit → Undo) containing

  • BSS-2 spikes: spikes of all driven neurons (hardware neuron indices, biological time), and
  • BSS-2 membrane voltage (neuron n): the membrane voltage of the neuron chosen under Record v of neuron. BSS-2 has a single MADC, so only one neuron's voltage is recorded per run. Its irregular samples are resampled to a regular time step; the values are raw MADC readings (a.u.).

Stop terminates the helper. A run already sent to the chip cannot be recalled; its results are discarded and you have to reconnect.

items.title: Rheobase routine
items.text:
The Design dynamic input → rheobase routine can run its probes on the chip: choose the target BrainScaleS-2 (neuromorphic). The dialog shows the connection state under the target; Connect connects with this tab's settings (container image, setup, token), so a routine can start without opening the tab once it is configured.

  • Each probe block (recovery, pulse, post-pulse window) is delivered as constant current, like Deliver does, with the tab's settings: container, setup, speed-up and i_offset max.
  • Probe amplitudes are fractions (0-1) of i_offset max, so a probe of 0.5 drives half of it, whatever the other probes are. Stim neuron i is hardware neuron i, and the probed neuron's membrane voltage is recorded.
  • All probes of a run go into one data group, BSS-2 rheobase <date time>, each placed at its probe's time in the input array, so the spikes and the membrane voltage line up with the stimuli. The routine counts the probed neuron's spikes in the pulse plus the post-pulse window and continues its search.
  • Because each constant-current segment is its own hardware run starting from rest (see Constant current above), every probe starts from rest too; spikes after the current switches off are not recorded.
  • The chip's response is noisy near threshold (the same amplitude can spike in one run and not the next). Repeats per probe (3 by default on the hardware targets, 1 for Brian2) runs every amplitude several times and counts it as a response when most runs spike; the log lists each run's spikes.
  • If even the maximum amplitude cannot make a short pulse fire, the routine keeps the thresholds it found and marks that duration in the plot (red triangle). It goes on locating the chronaxie when the maximum is at least twice the rheobase, and otherwise finishes with the rheobase and says how far to raise the maximum. Raising i_offset max in this tab (up to 1022) gives the fractions more current.
  • Stop ends the search and ignores a probe still running; it does not kill the shared helper.

items.title: Debug log
items.text:
The Debug log box at the bottom of the tab records every step with a timestamp: the exact singularity exec … launch command and the variables NeuroSeq passes into the container, the helper process start and exit code, everything the container prints while its software environment activates, the helper's Python/package versions and quiggeldy settings, and (with Show protocol traffic on) every message exchanged with the helper, with arrays summarised by type and shape.

The EBRAINS token never appears in the log: NeuroSeq and the helper only report whether it was given and how many characters it has.

To report a connection problem, click Copy log. It copies the log together with the NeuroSeq version, host, Singularity version, connection state and the tab's settings, ready to paste into a message. The text in the log can also be selected and copied directly. Clear empties the log.

items.title: Verified against the EBRAINS container
items.text:
Checked in image_lab_latest.oci.sif (Python 3.11, PyNN 0.12.3, neo 0.13.3):

  • pynn.run(runtime) durations are hardware milliseconds; consecutive runs need pynn.reset() in between.
  • constant_current_enable, constant_current_i_offset (and constant_current_type) are HXNeuron parameters; CalibHXNeuronCoba does not have them, so delivery uses HXNeuron on top of the nightly calibration (pynn.setup(initial_config=calib)).
  • HXNeuron records spikes, v, exc_synin, inh_synin, adaptation; SpikeSourceArray, OneToOneConnector and StaticSynapse exist.
  • hxcomm.ManagedConnection().get_unique_identifier() returns a list; the first entry is the chip identifier.
  • The helper starts through NeuroSeq's launch command and answers ping.

items.title: Start-up time
items.text:
• Without squashfuse on the host, Singularity unpacks the whole .sif on every start (about 1.5 minutes). Build an unpacked copy once and choose that folder as the container image instead (the container then starts in about 1 s):
singularity build --sandbox image_lab_latest_sandbox image_lab_latest.oci.sif
  • Activating the container's spack environment takes about 50 s. NeuroSeq caches the activation (spack env activate --sh) per image in the user cache folder (~/.cache/neuroseq/bss2 on Linux), so only the first connection after installing or updating an image pays this; later connections start in seconds.

items.title: Results on the chip
items.text:
Measured on hxcube7fpga0chip57_1 (quiggeldy.bioai.eu:11750, October 2026):

  • Chained APPEND runs do not work with this software version: only the first chained part was executed and recorded (membrane data stopped after it; later pulses produced no spikes), whether only constant_current_enable or also constant_current_i_offset changed between parts. Delivery therefore runs one hardware run per segment.
  • One run per segment works: each neuron fires only while its current is on, and constant_current_i_offset can change from segment to segment (one neuron: 200 → 0 spikes, 500 → 5, 1000 → 15 spikes per 0.1 ms).
  • Recording spikes of the population and v of one neuron in the same run works; the membrane is sampled every ≈32 ns of hardware time (≈32 µs biological at speed-up 1000).
  • Neurons differ: at the same i_offset they fire at different rates (2–9 spikes per 100 ms pulse at i_offset 500 in the staircase test), as expected for analog circuits.

items.title: In-App LLM Assistant (Experimental)
items.text:
!!! warning "Experimental feature" The in-app chat assistant is experimental and under active development. Behaviour, UI, supported providers, and the project context it receives may change without notice. It is not enabled in the default install.

NeuroSeq ships with an optional chat panel that lets you talk to an LLM about the currently loaded project. The assistant is given a snapshot of the project state (model, stimuli, experiments) as context and replies in a side panel next to the main window.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
The assistant lives behind the chat extra, which pulls in the provider SDKs and keyring for credential storage.

From the repository directly (requires SSH access to GitHub):

pip install "neuroseq[chat] @ git+ssh://git@github.com/neuroseq/neuroseq.git"

From a local checkout:

pip install ".[chat]"

Without the chat extra the panel is hidden and no LLM code paths run.

items.title: Configuring a provider
items.text:
Open Settings → LLM assistant to choose a provider and model. Three backends are bundled:

Provider Notes Ollama Local models served by a running Ollama daemon. OpenAI OpenAI API, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via the base URL field. Anthropic Anthropic Claude API.

For OpenAI and Anthropic you can paste an API key into the settings dialog. Keys are stored in the OS keyring via the keyring package; if no keyring backend is available NeuroSeq falls back to the OPENAI_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variables.

For Ollama you only need the base URL of the daemon (default http://localhost:11434) and the name of a pulled model.

items.title: Using the assistant
items.text:
Toggle the chat panel from the Chat action in the toolbar (robot icon). Type a message and press Send; replies stream in token by token. Each new message includes a fresh snapshot of the current project so the model can answer questions about the loaded simulation and data.

The assistant can request read-only details from the loaded project: model equations, parameters, initial conditions, synapses, monitors, runtime state, stimuli, experiments, and imaging metadata. Large arrays are read in pages of flattened values, with shape and units supplied where available. It can also list and read Python files within the installed neuroseq source package, including example projects. Files elsewhere on your computer are not accessible.

Requested project data and source text are sent to your selected provider. With a hosted provider, this includes the requested experimental data. Reads reflect the project at the time of each request. Stop cancels further requests; files already saved remain on disk.

To create an analysis plugin, ask the assistant, for example: "Create an analysis plugin that plots the mean trace across selected neurons." Before anything is saved, NeuroSeq shows a confirmation dialog with the target path and the complete code (or, for an update, a diff against the current file). The file is written only if you click Save plugin; if you cancel, the assistant is told that you declined. Review the code before accepting: tool results can contain text from shared project files, so a malicious project could try to steer the assistant into proposing harmful code.

Chat-authored plugins are saved only in your per-user plugin folder (for example ~/.local/share/neuroseq/analysis_plugins on Linux; override with the NEUROSEQ_USER_PLUGIN_DIR environment variable), never in the NeuroSeq package. Names starting with _ and names of built-in plugins are rejected, and only plugins already in your folder can be overwritten. Python syntax is checked before saving; this does not verify scientific correctness or runtime behavior. Reopen the right-click analysis menu to discover the new plugin. Discovery imports the Python code.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Project and source access is read-only except for Python files in the analysis plugin folder. The assistant cannot directly execute Python or run simulations.
  • Inspection uses a JSON request protocol supported by all three backends; reliability depends on the model following that protocol. Each turn allows up to 12 read/write requests; ask a follow-up to continue. Data is read on demand rather than sending the entire project and source tree in every prompt.
  • Conversations are not persisted across sessions.
  • Provider availability, model lists, and rate limits depend entirely on the chosen backend.

items.title: Experiment workflow
items.text:
1. Create experiment definition.
  2. Attach model and stimulus arrays.
  3. Run and record outputs.
  4. Export and compare results.

items.title: Managing project data
items.text: File → Manage Data opens the data manager dialog, which lists project data grouped by simulation run or recording and lets you inspect or delete selected groups (see Connecting simulations and experiments for details).

items.title: Generating synthetic data (GUI)
items.text:
File → Generate Synthetic Data… (Ctrl+G) opens a dialog that produces synthetic patch-clamp traces or imaging traces directly inside the project, useful for prototyping analyses without a real recording.

The dialog has two groups:

items.title: Patch clamp
items.text:
• Select traces — which template trace shapes to draw from.
  • Indexes to import — which neurons receive synthesized traces.
  • Noise (mV) — gaussian noise standard deviation added on top.

items.title: Imaging
items.text:
Choose Indicator response to control the fluorescence response to each spike:

  • Exponential decay (default) preserves the instantaneous rise followed by exponential decay.
  • Rise and decay uses a difference of exponentials with a gradual rise. Rise time constant (s) defaults to 0.010 s and must be shorter than Decay time (s), which defaults to 0.050 s. These settings give a peak about 20.1 ms after an isolated spike. The rise constant is not the time to peak.

For both models, dF/F sets the mean peak fluorescence change of an isolated spike before sampling and noise. Overlapping spike responses add together. The response is calculated at 0.1 ms resolution before sampling at the selected imaging rate, so a sampled trace may miss the exact peak. Both Export as a file and Add to the project use the selected response model.

  • Select spikes — source spike pattern that drives the synthetic fluorescence.
  • Recording duration / Number of neurons — output shape.
  • F0 (photoelectrons), dF/F, dF/F variability, Decay time (s), Sampling rate (Hz) — calcium-indicator parameters.
  • Lognormal mean / sigma (F0 distribution) — distribution from which per-neuron baseline brightness is drawn.
  • Photoelectron noise factor — shot-noise scaling.

A Data Preview panel updates as you change parameters so you can see what will be added before committing. The generated traces are appended to the project as a new experiment.

items.title: Cellpose test data (CLI)
items.text:
To generate synthetic Cellpose test data (TIFF image + matching .npy segmentation) outside the GUI:

neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_test_grid.tif

See Multiphoton Holographic Stimulation → Generating test data for the full set of options.

items.title: Export stimuli for patch clamp recordings
items.text:
A user can export stimuli from a given stimulation array to be used in patch clamp experiments. The most most universal format for export is *.csv supported by a large variety of 3rd party software.

The dialog for export can be found in File → Export → Patch Clamp Input. The pre-dialog asks for the export format — Igor2 - single array (.ibw / .csv) or Igor2 - all arrays (.pxp). A single-array export uses the input array currently shown in the editor; the user can then indicate the index of a neuron that was patched and the desired file format (default is .csv file).

More specific data formats tailored to a given 3rd party software may be provide an advantage in automatization and speed up data transfer from Neuroseq to this software. Below, we consider a concreate example(s) of integration with currently availibe hardwave/software for patch clamp recordings.
path: Export stimuli for patch clamp recordings

items.title: SutterPatch®- Igor Pro&reg
items.text:
The operation Sutter amplifiers is controlled via SutterPatch software run in the Igor Pro environment.

The generation of stimuli in Igor Pro environment is controled in "Routine Editor". There, a single routine in the routine pool can be modified to represent a given sequence of stimulations composed from distinct segments. A user will need only a single segment setting in to "Template" as a type of stimuli. The *.csv file created by Neuroseq for SutterPatch can be imported in a form of a Template.

The environment also has its own file format .ibw to store a stimuli of arbitraty shape. Neuroseq can directly generate the files of this format and facilitates import to SutterPatch. In this case, .ibw file with a sequence can be directly imported via Tempate Editor by cliking "Import":

The imported template will become availible in routine editor in the list of availible templates.
path: Export stimuli for patch clamp recordings

items.title: Project tabs
items.text: Every open project lives in its own tab. New, Open Project, opening an example project and dropping a .nseq file each open a new tab and leave the other tabs untouched; closing a tab with unsaved changes asks whether to save first. Menus and toolbars always act on the current tab. Only one simulation can run at a time across all tabs (Brian2's random seed and code-generation settings are shared), so starting a second one shows a notice instead.

items.title: File menu
items.text:
All data import and export actions are grouped under two sub-menus:

  • File → Import data
  • Input → Optogenetics — SysCon2 .seq import (see Multiphoton Holographic Stimulation)
  • Input → Patch Clamp — Igor2 .ibw / .pxp or .csv / .txt input waveform import (see Importing Igor2 Waves)
  • Output → Calcium Imaging (raw .tif) — raw 2-photon TIFF through the Cellpose + Suite2p pipeline
  • Output → Calcium Imaging (Suite2p outputs) — Suite2p fluorescence import
  • Output → Patch Clamp — patch-clamp recording (trace) import
  • File → Export
  • Patch Clamp Input — Igor2 stimulus CSV/.ibw/.pxp export for SutterPatch (see Export stimuli for patch clamp recordings)
  • Optogenetic Input — SysCon2 .seq (or Igor2) export for holographic hardware (see Multiphoton Holographic Stimulation). This only writes files; to also import the sequence into a connected SysCon2, use Export with settings… in the Stimulation setup panel.

File → Cell segmentation imports or runs Cellpose segmentation, and File → Manage Data lists the imported and simulated data groups so they can be deleted.

items.title: Undo and redo
items.text: Undo/redo covers input-array edits, deleting data groups in File → Manage Data, and imports into the project. The history belongs to the project tab and lasts for the session; it is not saved in the .nseq file.

items.title: Dropping files
items.text:
Files can also be dragged from the file explorer onto the NeuroSeq window. Each opens its usual import dialog with the file already loaded, so the imported data can be named and checked first:

File Dropped on Import .nseq anywhere opens the project in a new tab .seq anywhere SysCon2 sequence as an input array .ibw, .pxp, .csv, .txt the input array editor patch-clamp input wave .ibw, .pxp, .csv, .txt anywhere else patch-clamp traces TIFF or PNG the Cell segmentation tab asks for the Cellpose model, then segments TIFF the traces calcium trace extraction (Suite2p or ROI) TIFF, GIF or movie the Imaging tab adds it as imaging data TIFF, PNG, GIF or movie anywhere else asks which of the three imaging imports

items.title: General Layout
items.text:
The main layout of NeuroSeq consist of several widgets: the main widget for modification (drawing) of stimulation patterns (1), the widgets for visulisation of neuronal activity in form of traces (2) or spikes (3), monitor of synaptic connectivity (4). It also include a pad to quickly show some relevant analysis plots (5) and a GUI console (6).

The navigation in widgets (1-3) can be done with scrolling sliders or by holding a middle mouse button and moving the field of view of a given widget. By default, the field of new in all widgets is connected.

Zooming in and zooming out is done by corresponding "+" and "-" buttons or by holding "ctrl" or "shift" buttons and rotating mouse wheel for x- and y-axis, respectively.

Each widget can be shown or hidden in menu "View" by using the corresponding toolbar:

In addition to elements 1-6, the toolbar contains a universal widget that can dupicate widgets (2) and (3), useful for subsequent visulisation and data analysis. The button with capital "T" toggles and untoggles text annotation next to a mouse cursor — turn it off when the per-pixel coordinate label gets in the way of dense plots, and back on when you need it for precise selection.

View → Show Stimulation setup opens the stimulus-delivery pane, with one tab per target: SysCon2 (HOLO4D) for the holographic stimulation rig (see Multiphoton Holographic Stimulation) and BrainScaleS-2 for the neuromorphic chip (see Deliver stimuli to BrainScaleS-2).

View → Toggle Grid turns the time/neuron grid overlays on or off for the stim editor. The grid spacing follows the stim array's dt, so it doubles as a sample ruler.

items.title: Saving and loading
items.text:
Open project (Ctrl+O) and Save project (Ctrl+S) operate on .nseq archives. Both run in a background worker thread, so the main window stays responsive while large projects serialize. A progress dialog appears for any operation that takes more than a fraction of a second and exposes a Cancel button — cancelling a save leaves the original file untouched.

Once a project has been saved at least once, Save project (Ctrl+S) writes straight back to that same file — no dialogs, everything included. Use Save project As... to instead pick a new file (or different components to include, via the save-options dialog) without touching the original file. A brand-new, never-saved project always goes through Save project As...'s dialogs the first time, regardless of which of the two actions triggered it.

The project may contrain not only one, but several stimulation arrays. The user can select which one to show in the widget one, using a drop down manu in the "Stim data:" section of the folloing toolbar:

.

Similarly, the trace, spike and synapce data may contain a list of different data entries (generated in computational, biologial or neuromorphic experiments) with corresponding drop down menues. "All data" corresponds to a universal widget where any data in a form of traces or spikes can be independently selected.

.

items.title: Stimulation editor
items.text:
The stimulatation pattern can be edited using the toolbar located at the left side of a main window. The editing can be operated in draw and select modes.

In the drawing mode, the user can switch between "draw stimulus" and "erise stimulus" regimes and choose the amplitude and duration of the a drawn stimuli. The amplitude of a stimulus can be constant, gradient and log-gradient and random.

.

Mouse can be used for drawing stimuli: left click is drawing and right click is erising. In erise mode, the functionality of the left and right buttons is inverted. A longer stimulus can be drawing by holding a mouse button.

The intensity of stimulation is coded with transparency and normalized on the maximum value in an array. In the following example the relative ampitudes of stimuli are shown as 1 : 0.75 : 0.5 : 0.25 : 0.125 :

.

If "select mode" is active, the drawing options are not availible anymore, insteed other options are availible for selecting, copying, cutting, saving selected region and so on. The user can "do" and "undo" modifications in the editor using the corresponding buttons.

The toolbar also contains a pad with for creating/deleting new stim arrays, modifying the properties of the existing stimulation array (name, type, number of neurons and physical units) and padding/trimming the duration of an existing array.

The option "show all stim arrays" gives a possibility to show all stim arrays at the same time in one widget. In this case, the selected array remains the same, while other arrays will be shown in background with additional transparency applied.

items.title: Neuron data and spike data widgets
items.text:
Once the simulation is run or trace data is exported, it became availible in drop down menu "Neuron data". Natigation is done as described above. Normalization of traces can be set with buttons next it with a possibility to normalize traces on a median value and clip/upclip them to permit to restrict traces to the provided space for each neuron or provide a possibility to occupy an unlimited space within the widget. Spike data widget is analogous to the neuron data widget but constructed to represent binary spike events.

The data-selection toolbar has dedicated Trace normalization and Synapse normalization buttons (vertical-double-arrow icons) that open the per-widget normalization dialogs — median normalization, clip/unclip range, and per-neuron scaling all live in those dialogs rather than in the Settings menu.

items.title: Cell spatial footprints
items.text:
The Cell segmentation tab shows the imported Cellpose cells, labelled with their neuron ids. With the mouse:

  • Left click a cell to select it; the trace, input array and spike plots then show only the selected neurons. Click it again to deselect it.
  • Right drag around cells to select several at once (lasso).
  • Double-click empty space to clear the selection.
  • Right click a cell to scroll the traces to its neuron. The vertical zoom stays the same and all other traces stay visible. A neuron whose trace is hidden by the current selection is not scrolled to.

items.title: Synaptic data widget
items.text:
The synaptic data widget contains the information about the states of synaptic connections in a given time point. Using the replay mechanism described below one can access the modifications of synapic changes.

For large networks the full synapse matrix can be too big to render in real time. Settings → Synapse matrix RAM limit sets the memory budget (in MB); when the matrix would exceed it, the widget transparently downsamples along the time axis before rendering. The accompanying Heatmap widget (toggled via View → Show Heatmap) gives a 2D heatmap view of the same synaptic weight matrix.

items.title: Universal widget
items.text: During analysis, it may be desirable to show an additional copy of the widget, for example, to compare two different periods or neuronal populations within the same widget and at the same time. For this a universal "all data" widget was constructed.

items.title: Playback controls
items.text:
The Playback menu (and its mirror in the toolbar) drives the time cursor across every visualization widget simultaneously:

Action Shortcut Behaviour Set playback speed Opens a dialog to choose a playback rate multiplier. Skip to start Jumps the cursor to t = 0 without affecting play/pause state. Stop Pauses playback and rewinds the cursor to t = 0. Play / Pause Space Toggles continuous playback at the configured speed. Skip to end Jumps the cursor to the last simulated/recorded timepoint.

The time slider underneath the widgets stays clickable while playback is running, so you can scrub manually at any time.

items.title: Settings menu
items.text:
The Settings menu groups preferences that affect the rest of the application:

Setting What it does Brian2 simulation backend Pick cython (default) or numpy (see Simulations). Input automatic padding Default duration (seconds) used when creating new stim arrays and as a prefill for the Pad stim array dialog. LLM assistant Configure provider, model, and API key for the in-app chat assistant (experimental). Synapse matrix RAM limit Memory budget for rendering the full synaptic weight matrix; controls when the synapse and heatmap widgets switch to downsampled mode. Theme Switch between a Light, Dark and Retro light theme (beta) (the default) appearance. The choice is remembered and re-applied on the next launch.

The Retro light theme (beta) is the default on a fresh install. It is a skin in the spirit of the classic Winamp light skins: brushed-metal chrome with bevelled buttons, and dark LCD read-outs for the plot canvases, the console and the status bar. It is still marked beta — some dialogs are less polished than under the light and dark themes — and switching to Light or Dark is remembered like any other theme choice.

items.title: Analysis widget
items.text: The user can select a given region of the "neuron data" widget and access an analysis menu by right click of a mouse, and choosing a desired analysis plot/routine. The result lands in the dedicated Custom analysis dock widget — toggled from View → Show Custom analysis — or, with the (new window) variant of the action, in a separate window. See Analysis Tools and Custom Plugins for the full list of built-in analyses and how to write your own plugin.

items.title: GUI Console
items.text:
The GUI console is a text box at the bottom of the GUI that can be used to run a custom Python code.

A "Sample python code" button sits directly below the console input box. Clicking it opens a reference dialog with ready-to-use code snippets covering the most common tasks: listing and accessing stimulus arrays, editing values (zeroing, range assignment, generating waveforms), and accessing experiment and trace data. All snippets can be selected and copied directly into the console input box.

The code is executed in the same Python environment as the GUI, with the following variables/objects made available (run dir() command to see the list):

  • np: numpy
  • b2: brian2
  • stims: a dict of stimuli, each of which is a 2d numpy array
  • model: a class that defines the entire model

The console also has a history feature, which can be accessed by pressing the up and down arrow keys.

items.title: Stimuli Editing
items.text:
One of the purposes of the console is to allow users to modify the numpy arrays of stimuli using numpy and Python code. Any changes you make to the stimuli will be checked for validity, and if valid then they will be updated in the model and the changes will be displayed in the GUI, e.g.

>>> stims['stimulus'] = np.random.randint(2,size=(500, 24))

Example for generating a simple sequential stimulation pattern:

>>> for i in range(100):
...     project.stim_arrays['stimulus'].values[0+i*10:10+i*10,i] = 1

If the changes are invalid, then an error message will be displayed in the console, and the model will not be modified, e.g.

>>> stims['stimulus'] = np.random.randint(2,size=(5, 5, 5))
    Invalid stims: expected dict[str, 1d or 2d numpy array], found dict with 3d numpy array for key 'stimulus'

items.title: Model and brian2 objects
items.text:
The objects from the underlying brian2 model can also be accessed. For example, you can get a list of monitors with

>>> project.b2_model.monitors.keys()
dict_keys(['Traces_v', 'spikemon', 'synmon'])

And you can then get the underlying brian2 monitor object with e.g.

>>> monitor = project.b2_model.get_monitor('Traces_v')['object']
