Note that these objects should not be directly modified using the console, as it will cause the GUI and model to become out of sync with the underlying brian2 model.

It is also possible to modify other aspects of the model using the console, by interacting with the project.b2_model object. Try help(project.b2_model) to see what methods and attributes are available.

items.title: Importing Igor2 Waves
items.text:
NeuroSeq can import stimulation waveforms from Igor Pro / Sutter workflows into stimulation arrays.

Open the dialog from File → Import data → Input → Patch Clamp. The file picker accepts .ibw, .pxp, .csv, and .txt files.

items.title: Supported input formats
items.text:
CSV recordings can also be imported through File → Import data → Output → Patch Clamp by picking a .csv or .txt file. Both extensions use the same importer. Each column is a separate trace and each row is a sample. Comma, tab, and whitespace separators are detected automatically. An optional header row names the traces; without it, names use the filename and column number. Set the shared Source sampling rate in Hz, experiment, and recorded signal units. Tables import all columns as new traces with consecutive neuron IDs starting at the selected neuron ID. All columns are treated as signals, so remove any time column before import. Column names must be non-empty and unique; all rows must contain the same number of finite numeric samples.

For example, this imports traces named cell_a and cell_b:

cell_a,cell_b
-65,-62
-64,-61
-63,-60

For CSV patch-clamp input, choose File → Import data → Input → Patch Clamp and pick a .csv or .txt file. Both extensions accept a single column with one numeric sample per row; an optional first row can contain the waveform name. Without a header, the file name supplies the waveform name. Set Source sampling rate in Hz and choose the input units before importing. The preview and imported duration use this sampling rate. All samples are preserved, and the input array uses the source sample interval (dt = 1 / sampling rate).

  • .ibw: a single Igor Binary Wave
  • .pxp: an Igor Packed Experiment containing one or more waves
  • .csv: NeuroSeq's simple Igor-style CSV import format

Only one-dimensional waves can be imported into NeuroSeq stimulation arrays. Multi-dimensional waves inside a packed experiment are skipped.

items.title: Packed experiments (.pxp)
items.text:
When you open a .pxp file, NeuroSeq scans the packed experiment and lists all importable 1-D waves in a Wave Selection panel.

  • If the file contains exactly one importable wave, it is selected automatically.
  • If the file contains multiple waves, choose one from the list before importing.
  • Wave names are shown using their packed-experiment folder path, for example root/stims/HodgkinHuxley.

Once a wave is selected, the rest of the import workflow is the same as for .ibw and .csv.

items.title: When some records cannot be parsed
items.text:
Real-world .pxp files occasionally contain wave records whose stored shape does not match the data bytes on disk (for example, dependency-formula waves written without a full data block). NeuroSeq loads such files tolerantly: the malformed record is skipped and logged at WARNING level, and the remaining waves are still imported.

If any records were skipped, a warning dialog lists the count after the file is opened. The wave picker still populates with every wave that loaded successfully, and the application log records each skipped record's index, type, and reason.

items.title: Preview and timing
items.text:
After selecting a wave, the preview shows:

  • wave name
  • source format
  • source sample count
  • detected source sample interval (dt) when present
  • units and axis units
  • value range
  • optional Igor note text

For CSV files, set the source sampling rate in Hz before import. For Igor binary files, the source sample interval is read from the file.

Stimuli and recorded traces are imported at the source sample interval without resampling. Each new array or trace dataset stores its own dt, so different acquisition rates can coexist in one project and align by time in the plots.

items.title: Import targets
items.text:
The dialog offers two modes:

  • Create new stim array — creates a new single-neuron StimArray from the imported wave. Suggested name and units default to the Igor wave name and units.
  • Import into existing stim array — writes the imported wave into one selected neuron column of an existing stimulation array. Options:
  • Target neuron index selects which column to write.
  • Extend target stim array to fit imported duration grows the target in time if the imported wave is longer. Otherwise overflow samples are truncated.
  • Replace target neuron values instead of adding to them clears the destination column before writing. When unchecked, imported values are added sample-by-sample to the existing column.
  • Other neuron columns are always preserved.

If an existing target stimulation array or trace dataset uses a different dt than the source, NeuroSeq asks how to proceed:

  • Resample wave to target Δt (default) — the wave is resampled onto the target's grid; the target is unchanged.
  • Remap target to wave Δt — the whole target is remapped onto the wave's grid. Existing timing may shift by up to one sample, and remapping onto a fast recording's grid can make the target very large.
  • Cancel — nothing is imported.

Other datasets keep their intervals. The import is recorded as one undoable edit.

For packed experiments, the suggested stim name and units update automatically when you choose a different wave.

items.title: Current limitations
items.text:
• Import is still one wave at a time, even for .pxp files.
  • Packed-experiment metadata is not reconstructed into higher-level Sutter routine structures; NeuroSeq only imports the contained waves.

items.title: Importing imaging data
items.text:
NeuroSeq accepts imaging data from two distinct sources:

  • Cellpose — spatial cell segmentation (which pixels belong to which neuron). This is what NeuroSeq needs to map drawn stimuli back onto the physical sample for holographic export.
  • Suite2p — fluorescence traces extracted from a calcium imaging recording. These appear as TraceData in the project alongside any simulated traces.

Patch-clamp electrophysiology imports are also covered here for completeness.

items.title: Cellpose segmentation
items.text: Open File → Cell segmentation. Dropping a TIFF or PNG on the Cell segmentation tab opens the same dialog and segments the image right away.

items.title: Dialog sections
items.text:
• File Selection — point at the Cellpose output (a NumPy .npy array of per-pixel segmentation IDs, or the _seg.npy file produced by the Cellpose GUI).
  • Select file for segmentation… — segments a mean-fluorescence TIFF or PNG with the chosen Cellpose model and loads the result. The files are saved beside the image with the model in their name, e.g. fov_cpsam_seg.npy and fov_cpsam_cp_masks.png, so segmenting with another model keeps the earlier results, and an fov_seg.npy made in the Cellpose GUI is not overwritten. With Adjust brightness first ticked, the image is shown with the Brightness/Contrast controls of the Spatial Footprints panel before Cellpose runs, and Cellpose segments the adjusted image; Reset keeps the original. The window used is stored in the _seg.npy.
  • Data Information — read-only summary: image dimensions, number of detected cells, value range.
  • ID Mapping Options — choose how Cellpose IDs are mapped onto the project's neuron indices:
  • By ID — use the segmentation IDs as-is.
  • By order — renumber sequentially in the order Cellpose found cells.
  • Custom shape mapping — assign each cell to a target neuron index via a SquareAOI or CircleAOI overlay role. Use this when the project's neuron layout (e.g. a grid of square AOIs) does not match Cellpose's discovery order.
  • Areas of Interest — optional roles drawn on top of the segmentation (square/circle AOIs). Cells that fall inside an AOI inherit its role. The Linear strategy shows the same shapes, which can be moved and resized there too, but they do not change its mapping; they are kept with the imported segmentation.

After import, the cell footprints are available in the cell overlay widget and are bundled into the project file. They are required for the SysCon2 holographic export.

items.title: Cell overlay widget
items.text:
The cell overlay widget visualizes the imported segmentation on top of the sample image. You can:

  • Pan and zoom with the mouse wheel and middle-button drag, matching the other widgets.
  • See cells that have been mapped to project neurons highlighted relative to unmapped ones.
  • Drag the corner/edge handles of square and circle AOI overlays to refine their position after import — the cell-to-neuron assignment recomputes whenever an AOI moves.

items.title: Showing one channel of a movie
items.text: Movies recorded with several channels store them interleaved frame by frame, so playing every frame makes the Imaging tab flicker between channels. Set Channels in the Imaging tab's bottom bar to the number of channels and pick the one to watch under Show; All frames plays every frame in file order. The frame rate entered on import is the rate of each channel, so one channel plays in step with the time slider. Imports through the TIFF pipeline start with its channel count and functional channel. The choice is saved per imaging data entry. ScanImage recordings use Functional channel in the ScanImage (imaging) tab of the Stimulation setup pane instead.

items.title: Saving imaging data
items.text:
Save imaging data… in the Imaging tab first asks which frames to save. Frames are counted from 1, as in the time slider tooltip and in Fiji; Current frame fills in the frame shown at the slider position, so a short period found by scrubbing can be saved directly. Choose what to save:

  • Original frames (TIFF substack) — the recorded pixel values of the shown channel, as one stack that Fiji opens with its frame interval.
  • With stimulation marks (TIFF or GIF) — the frames as displayed, with the stimulated cells marked by a red "x" sized to the image. All saved frames share one grey scale, taken from robust percentiles of the saved frames, so the background does not flicker from frame to frame.

items.title: Generating test data
items.text:
If you do not have a real recording yet, NeuroSeq can synthesize a Cellpose test image with a clean grid of cells:

neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_test_grid.tif \
  --cellpose-grid-rows 10 \
  --cellpose-grid-cols 10 \
  --cellpose-radius 11 \
  --cellpose-gap 30

See Multiphoton Holographic Stimulation → Generating test data for the full set of options.

items.title: GPU acceleration (Cellpose & Suite2p)
items.text:
Both Cellpose segmentation and the Suite2p extraction/deconvolution step run on PyTorch and are dramatically faster on a GPU. NeuroSeq uses the GPU automatically when one is available — CUDA on NVIDIA cards or MPS on Apple Silicon — and otherwise falls back to the CPU (which can be unusably slow for segmentation).

Two things are required: a GPU that these tools support, and a GPU build of PyTorch. Cellpose can use only NVIDIA (CUDA) and Apple (MPS) GPUs — Intel integrated graphics (Iris Xe / UHD) are not supported.

Check what you have (in the NeuroSeq environment):

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"

A version ending in +cpu (e.g. 2.13.0+cpu), or False, means a CPU-only build is installed — the Cellpose "use GPU" option will be greyed out.

Enable the GPU (on a machine with an NVIDIA or Apple-Silicon GPU) by installing a GPU build of PyTorch into the NeuroSeq environment:

uv pip install --torch-backend=auto torch

uv auto-detects the machine's CUDA driver and installs the matching wheel. On Windows this step is required, because PyPI's default torch wheel is CPU-only there (on Linux the default PyPI wheel is already CUDA-enabled). A later uv sync can revert to the CPU build; re-run the command, or set UV_TORCH_BACKEND=auto in the environment. Verify with the check command above (expect e.g. 2.x.x+cu128 True), then relaunch NeuroSeq.

If NeuroSeq is installed into an environment uv doesn't manage (e.g. a conda environment), install a CUDA build directly with pip instead:

pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

Pick the cuXXX index matching your NVIDIA driver if cu128 doesn't fit (check the PyTorch install page).

No supported GPU (e.g. an Intel-only laptop)? GPU segmentation is not possible on that machine. Instead, run Cellpose on one machine that does have an NVIDIA/Apple GPU and import its _seg.npy output (the file-selection path above needs only the segmentation, not a GPU), and/or use a lighter Cellpose model or downsample the image before segmenting.

When a GPU is unavailable, NeuroSeq shows a one-time hint after launching Cellpose and logs the same information before running the Suite2p pipeline.

items.title: Raw calcium imaging TIFFs
items.text: File → Import data → Output → Calcium Imaging (raw .tif) extracts traces directly from one or more 2-photon TIFF stacks. Choose the Cellpose masks (those already loaded in the project, a _seg.npy file, or Suite2p auto-detection), the pipeline (Suite2p, or a simple ROI average) and the acquisition parameters, then Run pipeline. The pipeline runs in the background; the resulting traces are imported like Suite2p outputs.

items.title: Suite2p calcium imaging
items.text:
File → Import data → Output → Calcium Imaging (Suite2p outputs) opens the Suite2p importer.

  • File Selection — point at a Suite2p output folder (the directory that contains F.npy, Fneu.npy, iscell.npy, …). Individual file paths can also be supplied directly via the Individual File Selection group when the folder layout is non-standard.
  • Data Preview — shows a few representative traces so you can confirm the right cells are being imported before committing.
  • Import Options — neuropil subtraction, dF/F normalization, decimation, and which Suite2p classification mask (iscell) to apply.

Imported traces become a new TraceData entry under the project's experiments and appear in the Neuron data dropdown.

items.title: Patch-clamp electrophysiology
items.text:
File → Import data → Output → Patch Clamp loads recorded traces (voltage in current clamp, current in voltage clamp):

  • File Selection — an Igor2 .ibw / .pxp file, or a .csv / .txt table with one trace per column. Packed experiments list their waves in a Wave Selection panel; import as many as you need, then click Close.
  • Wave Preview and Source Wave Settings — check the wave and set the source sampling rate where the file does not store it.
  • Import Target — create new trace data or add to existing trace data. If the existing data uses a different sample interval, NeuroSeq offers to resample the wave (default) or remap the target, as described in Importing Igor2 Waves.
  • Spike detection — optional peak detection to derive a SpikeData alongside the trace.

For patch-clamp input (command) waveforms use File → Import data → Input → Patch Clamp; see Importing Igor2 Waves.

items.title: Multiphoton Holographic Stimulation (SysCon2 Export)
items.text: NeuroSeq can export stimulation patterns as SysCon2 .seq files for use with Holo4D multiphoton holographic stimulation hardware.

items.title: Overview
items.text: The stim array you draw in NeuroSeq represents laser TTL pulses directly. Each sample corresponds to one SysCon2 hardware tick (dt = 0.0005208125 s = 520.8125 µs). NeuroSeq infers the SLM shape objects needed for each neuron from the drawn TTL pulse positions — you do not need to manually define hologram boundaries.

items.title: Required setup
items.text:
Parameter Required value stim_array.dt 0.0005208125 s (one SysCon2 tick) Cellpose segmentation loaded and mapped to stimulus channels SysCon2 template a previously imported .seq file in the same session

The dialog will reject (or offer to fix) stim arrays whose dt does not match the SysCon2 tick quantum.

items.title: Drawing TTL pulses
items.text:
Draw active samples in the stimulation editor exactly where you want the laser to fire. A few rules apply:

  • No minimum duration: pulses can be as short as one tick (520.8 µs).
  • dt must be the SysCon2 tick: use the Fix dt button in the sanity-check dialog if you need to convert an existing array.
  • Blank lead-in required: the SLM hardware needs one full 16.666 ms window (32 ticks) of blank time before the first laser pulse to load the hologram. The sanity fixer inserts this automatically if it is missing, but you can also add it yourself with Shift right for initial SLM load.

items.title: How shape objects are derived
items.text:
The export pipeline maps your raw TTL pulses onto SLM shape objects as follows:

  1. Window coverage — each raw pulse is mapped to the 32-tick window(s) it falls in. This determines which SLM pattern windows must be loaded.
  2. Hologram grouping — active windows are grouped into holograms. A new hologram starts when the active neuron set changes relative to the previous non-empty window: either a neuron disappears or a new neuron appears. Gaps (fully empty windows) do not break the hologram — the pattern stays loaded across the gap.
  3. Pre-load blank window — a blank 16.666 ms window is placed immediately before the first active window of each hologram. The SLM uses this time to load the pattern before any laser pulse fires. If the blank is missing the sanitizer inserts one by shifting the tail right.
  4. Shape object bounds — for each neuron within a hologram:
  5. shape starts at (first_active_window - 1) × 32 ticks (the blank load window),
  6. shape ends at last_active_window_excl × 32 ticks (minimum span: load + 1 active window).

items.title: TTL pulse timing
items.text:
Laser TTL pulses are emitted at exact tick positions, not at window boundaries. If a pulse was drawn at tick 100, the exported .seq file contains a TTLPulse starting at tick 100 (= 52.08 ms).

If the sanitizer inserted a blank window before the first active window (because the first pulse was too early), all raw pulse positions are shifted by 32 ticks per inserted blank. The shift preserves the sub-window offset of each drawn pulse relative to its containing window.

Roundtrip accuracy — when a .seq file exported in this mode is imported back into NeuroSeq with dt = 0.0005208125 s, each pulse reconstructs at the same sample index it was exported from (sample_idx == tick_idx).

items.title: Hologram boundary rule
items.text:
Situation Effect Same neuron set, contiguous windows continue same hologram Same neuron set, gap between windows continue same hologram (SLM stays loaded) A neuron that was active in the last non-empty window disappears start new hologram A neuron that was never in the current hologram appears start new hologram

A new hologram is triggered whenever the active neuron set changes — either a neuron leaves or a new one joins relative to the last non-empty window. Gaps (fully empty windows) are ignored when checking for disappearances; only transitions between consecutive non-empty windows matter.

items.title: Sanity checks
items.text:
Run Check Input Sanity in the stimulation generator dialog before exporting. The checker validates:

  • dt is the SysCon2 tick quantum (offers Fix dt button if not),
  • first active sample is at least 32 ticks from the start (SLM lead-in),
  • no SLM gap violations between successive neuron groups,
  • no off→on SLM overlap violations,
  • no simultaneous neurons with mismatched durations (optional; use Equalize durations),
  • all active neurons have a valid Cellpose mapping.

Feedback is shown in a scrollable dialog. If fixes were applied you can write the corrected values back to the stim array via Apply fixes.

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
1. Open File → Export → Optogenetic Input and choose SysCon2 in the pre-dialog. This writes the files only; to also import the generated sequence into a connected SysCon2, use Export with settings… in the Stimulation setup panel instead.
  2. Select the stim array and Cellpose segmentation.
  3. Choose laser wavelength (940 nm, 1030 nm, or 1100 nm digital; default 940 nm).
  4. Optionally set a Target power and load a power LUT (see below).
  5. Click Check Input Sanity and resolve any errors.
  6. Enter an output script name and click Export.

The output folder starts as the one used last, or Documents\NeuroSeq\SysCon exports the first time, so scripts can be generated without browsing for a folder. Scripts imported into SysCon2 go to its Target directory, which defaults to one folder per day, neuroseq\<date> (e.g. neuroseq\2026-10-15).

In the SysCon2 panel, the Target power box next to Export current array to stimulation setup sets the power of that quick export. Changing only the power there keeps all other settings of the last export; Export with settings… starts from the same value.

Export settings and the export folder belong to the project: they are saved with it and restored when you switch between open projects.

items.title: Target power and power LUT
items.text:
The dialog has a Target power (mW) spinner next to a Load LUT… button:

  • Setting Target power to 0 disables power control — the exported Intensity_0 fields are written as zero, which matches the historical default behaviour.
  • Loading a SysCon .lut file maps the requested mW to the laser's intensity percentage at the currently selected wavelength. The exporter divides that percentage by 100 for the .seq intensity fields (0–1). Each wavelength has its own LUT slot. The mW those fractions stand for are kept in each Shape's and laser pulse's description, e.g. neuron=3 power_mW=12.5 target_mW=25 (the requested power for that object, i.e. the target times its amplitude, and the target power).
  • LUTs are bundled into the .nseq archive when you save the project, so the export stays reproducible across machines. Loading a LUT marks the project as modified; save it to retain the calibration.

The status label next to the button shows which LUT (if any) is currently loaded for the active wavelength. Switching the wavelength combobox swaps to that wavelength's LUT slot.

The exporter writes:

File Content <name>.seq SysCon2 sequence — Shape objects + TTLPulse objects <name>_original_stim.npz the exported input array, restored on re-import <name>_overview.png timeline overview image

items.title: Generating test data (CLI)
items.text:
# 512 × 512 image with 10 × 10 grid
neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_512.tif \
 --cellpose-grid-rows 10 \
 --cellpose-grid-cols 10 \
 --cellpose-radius 11 \
 --cellpose-gap 30

# 1300 × 1300 with auto-fitted radius/gap
neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_1300.tif \
 --cellpose-grid-rows 10 \
 --cellpose-grid-cols 10 \
 --cellpose-square-size 1300

items.title: Importing a .seq file
items.text:
Use File → Import data → Input → Optogenetics to reconstruct a sequence in a new or existing input array. Browsing and cancelling do not change the project. Import applies the file's header as the session's export template only after conversion succeeds. The imported input uses 520.8125 µs samples. If an existing target input uses a different interval, only that input is resampled after confirmation. Other input arrays and trace datasets keep their own intervals and align by time in the plots.

Targets map to consecutive channels starting at Target neuron offset, in their first-occurrence order for Holo4D sequences. They are not matched to project neuron IDs or Cellpose identities. Repeated point Shapes at identical coordinates and with the same lightsource share a channel; nearby legacy Entities retain the 1 µm grouping rule. Multiple spots in one ROI may therefore import as separate channels. The preview shows the same grouping used for conversion.

Replace mapped target channels clears only channels receiving imported data; other channels are preserved. Disable it to merge using the maximum value at each sample. Dropped channels, clipped duration, and capped legacy repeats require confirmation before the project changes. Files that reconstruct no stimulation are rejected, as are arrays exceeding the 512 MiB import allocation limit.

Holo4D timing is reconstructed from each target's laser TTL pulses and SLM availability windows. The Legacy repeat tick setting does not change Holo4D's 520.8125 µs TTL quantum. One sequence pass is imported; the header's runs count is not expanded. Imported amplitudes are raw file intensity values, with a nominal 1 used for zero-intensity shapes, rather than recovered optical power or the original drawing amplitudes. Spiralling latency and hardware behavior cannot be inferred from the file, so this is not a measurement of delivered stimulation. Objects with multiple timing entries or multiple lightsources are rejected rather than partially imported.

Every export also writes <name>_original_stim.npz next to the .seq: the exact input array, including silent neurons. The .seq holds hardware-adjusted timings (SLM load delays), so importing it alone reproduces those adjusted timings. When the sidecar sits next to the file and still matches it, the import restores the original array with its exact timings and neuron rows. Keep the two files together.

items.title: Setup panel and hardware execution
items.text:
Export defaults are 940 nm, Force binary export intensity off, Spiralling off, Exact stimulus timing on, and Use 10 input spots per ROI on. With exact timing, each hologram shape starts one 16.7 ms SLM load window before its first pulse instead of on the window grid, and stimuli are delayed only where the previous hologram leaves no room for that load (the first stimulus is always delayed by one window). Untick it to snap shapes to the window grid, which can delay stimuli by up to a window per hologram. Previously remembered settings still apply to quick exports. With a linear 85 mW maximum calibration, 5 mW is exported as approximately 0.058824, not 5.8824, in both Shape and laser TTL intensity fields. Use the rig's measured wavelength-specific LUT; the linear example is not a replacement calibration.

Main-menu exports populate the setup panel's generated preview without importing into hardware. Exports from the setup panel import when connected. Routine blocks also update the preview after import acknowledgement. Preview images resize with the panel and remain distinct from hardware status.

Laser controls are currently read-only: Get Status discovers lightsources on its first use, preferring 940 nm, and retrieves status. The single selector displays friendly names while retaining the original SCI identifiers internally. Set power, shutter, and emission in SysCon2 itself.

Select the imported sequence, choose Runs and trigger settings, and click Upload. After confirmation of an endless upload, NeuroSeq uploads and waits for hardware Idle. Then click Run and confirm to start the sequence. The panel shows phases, elapsed time, and hardware Busy/Idle state; SCI provides no percentage-complete measurement. A triggered run remains waiting until Busy is observed. A short automatic run can finish between polls; that case is reported without claiming measured completion. Stop also cancels any queued Run.

The preview is collapsed by default; click Show preview to expand it.

The dynamic-routine dialogs offer Use SysCon2 dt and prompt for resampling when starting with the wrong timestep.

items.title: Dynamic input routines on the rig
items.text:
With the SysCon2 (calcium imaging) target, the rheobase and STDP window dialogs show Hardware settings: target power, laser, spiral scanning and spots per cell (the project's export settings, shared with the SysCon2 tab, so no Export with settings… is needed first), plus how blocks are recorded. With Run blocks automatically and record them with ScanImage, each block is uploaded and run by NeuroSeq while ScanImage records it, triggered by the sequence, and its ΔF/F traces are extracted with the project's Cellpose masks; see ScanImage acquisition. Rheobase then counts a probe as evoking a response, depending on Calcium readout, when the neuron's ΔF/F rises by the Response threshold within the post-pulse window, or when OASIS deconvolution of that ΔF/F finds a spike (an event of at least the Spike threshold) in it. Unticked, each block is only imported into SysCon2 and you run, record and import it yourself, then click Calcium data imported (rheobase can then measure the rise of an imported ΔF/F or raw fluorescence trace, e.g. the TIFF import's ROI averages, or deconvolved spikes; Suite2p's normalised traces are refused, since a rise relative to their baseline is meaningless). Export warnings are asked once per routine rather than failing every block. Since probe amplitudes are fractions of the target power, a routine refuses to send a block without a target power above 0 mW and a power LUT for the chosen laser, or with a target above the LUT's maximum (higher amplitudes would all be delivered at that maximum); every stimulated neuron must have a Cellpose ROI. Amplitudes must be above 0 and at most 1.

Choosing the SysCon2 target first gives rheobase settings for cells in a slice: a 16.7 ms pulse (one spiral; a shorter pulse with spiral scanning on is logged as a warning, since only part of the spiral is delivered), up to 100 ms, 1 s recovery, a 300 ms post-pulse window and Fixed duration, varying amplitude, since every probe is a recording. Each target keeps its own values when you switch back and forth. With deconvolved spikes, a spike in the imaging frame after the post-pulse window still counts: the frames lit by a short pulse are imputed, so its response first shows in full in the next frame. Simulations finishing or failing meanwhile do not affect a hardware run.

Each routine run keeps its block scripts in its own folder inside the project's export folder (the one Export with settings… used last), for example SysCon exports\rheobase_2026-10-22_143012\. Every block is saved there as rheobase_2026-10-22_143012_001.seq, with its overview PNG and stimulus sidecar, and imported into SysCon2 under the same name, so names never repeat across runs. A recording of a block records the path of its .seq. Scripts exported with Export current array to stimulation setup stay temporary and are deleted when NeuroSeq closes. The Create input array and Edit input array dialogs also provide exact presets for SysCon2 (520.8125 µs), 1 ms, 0.1 ms, 50 µs, and 30 Hz imaging.

items.title: Run External Simulators
items.text: NeuroSeq can run simulation backends that are outside the built-in Brian2 model. This is useful when a project should include models implemented with another frameworks or run external devices.

items.title: What an External Simulator Does
items.text: An external simulator receives the current stimulus arrays from the project, runs its own backend, and returns an Experiment. NeuroSeq then lets you import that result as a new experiment or append it to an existing one.

items.title: Connect an External Simulator
items.text:
To load a custom simulator from a Python file:

  1. Open the Experiment menu.
  2. Select Connect external stimulation function.
  3. Choose a Python file that exposes a compatible simulate(...) entry point.

NeuroSeq will load that file and store the connection in the current project.

items.title: Connecting a Brian2-based backend
items.text: There is a second entry, Experiment → Connect brian2 external stimulation function, for backends that themselves build a Brian2 network. The contract is the same — a Python file exposing simulate(...) — but NeuroSeq forwards the project's existing Brian2 unit system and preferred code-generation target (see Simulations → Choosing a Brian2 backend) to the loaded module. Use this when your external model needs to share Brian2 state or units with the rest of the project; otherwise the plain Connect external stimulation function is sufficient.

items.title: Run an External Simulator
items.text:
Once a simulator is connected:

  1. Prepare or edit the stimulus arrays in the Stimuli view.
  2. Open the Experiment menu.
  3. Select Run external stimulation function.
  4. Enter the simulation time.
  5. Choose whether to import the returned experiment as a new experiment or append it to an existing one.

If a project has an external simulator configured, the main Run simulation action can also dispatch to that simulator instead of Brian2.

items.title: Built-In Example: ELISE
items.text: The bundled ELISE Sequence Learning Network example project already comes connected to the ELISE backend. In that project, the external simulator is loaded automatically and uses the class-based NN backend entry point in src/neuroseq/example_models/elise.py.

items.title: What Data Is Passed to the Simulator
items.text:
NeuroSeq passes stimulus arrays as a dictionary of the form:

{
    "stim_name": {
        "array": ndarray,
        "dt": seconds,
    }
}

The backend returns an Experiment containing trace, spike, synapse, or other supported data objects.

items.title: Errors and Troubleshooting
items.text:
If loading fails, NeuroSeq shows an error dialog and clears the external simulator connection.

If execution fails, NeuroSeq shows an External Simulation error dialog. Common causes are:

  1. The Python file does not expose the expected entry point.
  2. The simulator expects a stimulus name that is not present in the project.
  3. The simulator raises an exception while building or advancing its backend state.

If you are implementing the simulator yourself, see developer/custom_simulators.md.

items.title: ScanImage acquisition on the same PC
items.text:
The ScanImage (imaging) tab of the Stimulation setup pane connects to a running ScanImage MATLAB session; the Image acquisition toolbar button shows it (as does View → Show Stimulation setup). It starts Focus, starts or externally arms a recording, aborts an acquisition, and opens completed TIFF files in the Imaging tab. ScanImage owns the scanner, its own live display and the original recording.

NeuroSeq does not stream live images. Fetching frames through MATLAB ran on the thread that also runs ScanImage and slowed acquisition down (issues #628, #651), so the tab has controls only; watch the image in ScanImage's display windows. Placing acquisition next to stimulation also lets the dynamic input routines drive both (see below).

This integration targets ScanImage Premium 2023.1.0, single-plane raster imaging. Its MATLAB adapter requires validation on the actual acquisition PC; automated Python tests do not establish hardware compatibility or timing. Volumes, FastZ, multi-ROI and arbitrary-line acquisitions are outside this initial implementation. A configured Z-stack is fine as long as stacks are disabled. For its own recordings NeuroSeq sets logging averaging and acquisitions per loop to 1, so every raw frame is saved in one acquisition, and restores your values when the recording ends, is aborted or fails to start. NeuroSeq uses Grab, not Loop, so the loop repeat period is not used.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
1. Start ScanImage normally and load the microscope's configuration. In that MATLAB window run:
matlab.engine.shareEngine('NeuroSeqScanImage')

  1. Prepare a separate Python installation compatible with that MATLAB release. NeuroSeq itself requires Python 3.12+, so do not install an incompatible engine into NeuroSeq's environment. For example, MATLAB R2023a supports Python 3.10; R2023b also supports Python 3.11. Consult the MathWorks compatibility table. Install MATLAB Engine matching the installed MATLAB release, plus numpy and tifffile, in the helper interpreter. A current unpinned engine package is not necessarily compatible with older MATLAB.

  2. Click Image acquisition in the toolbar, select that Python executable and enter the shared session name. Click Connect. The helper connects only to an existing session with that name; it never starts another MATLAB instance. Required ScanImage properties and user-function registration are probed. NeuroSeq remembers the Python executable as the default for next time; the recording folder is remembered per project (and the last one used becomes the default for new projects).

  3. Configure scanners, PMTs, saved/displayed channels and trigger wiring in ScanImage. Set Functional channel to the channel of the calcium indicator: it is the channel shown for recordings in the Imaging tab and the one dynamic input routines measure (it must be among the saved channels).

The bundled .m files are added to the MATLAB path for the session. The adapter registers acquisition lifecycle callbacks alongside existing user functions; it does not replace the user's callback table. Reconnecting reconciles the adapter's entries without duplicating them, including after clearing MATLAB functions. New callback registration requires ScanImage to be idle. A normal idle disconnect removes its callbacks. It does not shut down MATLAB.

items.title: Focus and recording
items.text:
Focus starts ScanImage's continuous unsaved imaging, shown in ScanImage. Abort Focus before starting a recording.

Choose a recording folder and frame count; the experiment name is optional. Save channels lists ScanImage's channels and starts with channel 1 ticked; tick several to record them together in one acquisition. ScanImage's own selection is restored after the recording, like the other settings NeuroSeq changes.

Every recording is one TIFF directly in the recording folder, named after the date and a recording number that continues from the files already there, e.g. 2026-10-22_00003.tif; Next file shows the name the next recording gets. NeuroSeq sets ScanImage's file stem to the date, its file counter to the recording number, and frames per file to unlimited, and restores them afterwards. A recording never overwrites an existing file. The experiment name, which keeps its capitalisation, names the recording's data group in the project; without one, the file name is used.

Record / Arm enables ScanImage TIFF logging. When Wait for external acquisition trigger is selected, ScanImage waits for its configured trigger input. Otherwise it starts through software. The first-frame timeout requests an abort if no acquisition start is observed. "Waiting for first frame" is not proof that hardware is ready to accept a TTL.

items.title: Field of view for cell segmentation
items.text:
Grab FOV for segmentation records a short recording (300 frames by default, started by software, without stimulation). The whole recording is kept as <date>_<number>.tif; its Functional channel is averaged into one image saved beside it as <date>_<number>_mean.tif. The cell segmentation dialog then opens and runs Cellpose on it. Because the image comes from the same scan, the masks share the recordings' pixel grid, as the dynamic input routines need. The snapshot is listed in the acquisition history but adds no data group or imaging entry.

NeuroSeq reports state from ScanImage, waits for completed/aborted acquisition events and readable, stable files, then indexes the saved channels and frame timestamps. A successful complete acquisition must contain the requested frame count. Should ScanImage still split a recording into several files, they are grouped as one recording. Aborted recordings with readable complete channel groups can also be attached, labeled as aborted. An externally triggered Grab can end through ScanImage's abort after its last frame, so an "aborted" recording that holds every requested frame counts as completed.

After completion, abort, or a failed start, the adapter restores the previous logging folder, filename stem/counter, frames per file, logging enable, external-trigger enable, and frames-per-slice settings once ScanImage is idle. If the terminal callback precedes the idle state, the next status poll retries restoration; idle Disconnect also restores pending settings, as do the next Preview and Record if ScanImage became idle without any terminal callback. Verify restoration on your rig, including after abort, before starting another manual Grab. Acquisition metadata retains the settings used during the recording.

A completed acquisition is added to the project that requested it and becomes its selected imaging data. Imported imaging data and earlier recordings stay in the list. The tab's Functional channel picks the channel shown for recorded playback. When the shown recording did not save it, its first saved channel is shown instead, with a message; the setting itself stays, since dynamic input routines measure that channel.

The imaging data selector next to Image acquisition lists all imaging data in the project: imported TIFF/GIF/movie files and finished recordings. Import Imaging Data adds to this list, and Remove imaging data removes only the selected entry. Files remain external to .nseq; moving them without restoring their paths makes playback unavailable. Projects save the run metadata and index, not the raw movie. Frame indexes use compact columns and file indices and are stored once per run; the selected movie references that run. Full frame descriptions remain in the original TIFFs and can be reread for future alignment analysis. Save the project to retain its acquisition history.

A small, human-readable <date>_<number>.json beside the TIFF stores the request, the stimulus it relates to (name, sample interval, shape and SHA-256 of its samples; the samples themselves are in <date>_<number>_stimulus.npy beside it, so the folder alone reproduces the stimulus), the block of a dynamic input routine (with the path of its .seq file and its SysCon2 sequence-manager entry), and the SysCon export settings. Both files are written before the hardware command, so they aid recovery if NeuroSeq exits before the project is saved, and both are removed again if ScanImage refuses to start. The requested state in the JSON is not evidence that the acquisition completed.

The existing Save imaging data… action exports a rendered derivative. It does not replace ScanImage's original TIFF recording. Recorded ScanImage playback uses channel-specific frame timestamps; brightness conversion affects only the display/derivative. GIF exports use the recorded inter-frame intervals, subject to GIF timing precision. Other movie formats use a constant frame rate and do not preserve irregular acquisition timing; retain the TIFF timestamps for analysis.

items.title: Stimulation and timing
items.text: For manual recordings, use the SysCon2 tab to export/select/upload stimulation. Imaging can be armed here and triggered through the configured physical input. Manual recordings are marked as having unverified synchronization: software command arrival times are not measured stimulation times, so planned stimulation crosses are suppressed for them. The 2023 auxiliary trigger feature can record stimulation markers on supported resonant systems. Their frame descriptions remain in the original TIFFs for a future calibrated alignment step.

items.title: Dynamic input routines
items.text:
With the SysCon2 target and Run blocks automatically and record them with ScanImage ticked in their hardware settings, the rheobase and STDP window routines run each block without manual steps:

  1. Export the block, import it into SysCon2, select it and upload it (1 run).
  2. Arm a ScanImage recording that waits for the external trigger, with enough frames for the block plus the Record after block time at ScanImage's frame rate.
  3. Run the sequence (start condition auto); its TTL output must trigger ScanImage, so the recording starts with the block.
  4. When the recording is complete, extract the ΔF/F trace of every cell with the project's Cellpose masks (frames lit by the stimulation laser are interpolated; F0 is the mean before the block's first stimulus), deconvolve it into spikes with OASIS (as Suite2p does, with jGCaMP8m's 0.5 s decay; an event of at least the Spike threshold, in ΔF/F, is a spike), and measure the response on this block's trace.
  5. Place both in the run's data group, named after the run folder (e.g. rheobase_2026-10-27_153313), at the block's time in the stim array. The run thus has one continuous ΔF/F trace and one spike dataset; a block overwrites the previous recording's tail where it starts. Each recording is still listed as imaging data, without a data group of its own.

A recording that has not finished 15 s after the block plus its Record after block time is aborted and the routine stops (the usual cause is a trigger that never reached ScanImage). The Functional channel measured starts at 1 in every session; check it before a run. STDP pairing blocks need no data, so they are run without recording. The routine needs SysCon2 and ScanImage connected, ScanImage's frame rate reported, and a Cellpose segmentation of the same field of view whose masks share the TIFFs' pixel grid. These recordings are marked stimulation_trigger synchronization. Verify the trigger wiring (the SysCon2 configuration's TargetConnectorPort) and the delay between sequence start and the first frame on the rig before relying on the measured windows.

items.title: Interruptions and rig acceptance
items.text:
An unresponsive helper is terminated after 30 seconds; MATLAB and the scanner are not killed. Acquisition state is then unknown. Inspect ScanImage before reconnecting. Closing NeuroSeq stops its helper transport; it does not promise to stop an independently running microscope acquisition. Use Abort acquisition and verify idle before closing when you intend to stop imaging.

Before experimental use, verify on the acquisition PC:

  • Previous ScanImage logging/trigger/frame-count settings are restored after completion, abort, failed start, and idle disconnect; a subsequent manual Grab uses the original settings.
  • The probe succeeds on the exact ScanImage/MATLAB build and reports settings.
  • Recorded playback orientation matches a known asymmetric target and the Cellpose masks of the same field of view.
  • Recordings are written as <date>_<number>.tif in the chosen folder, the number continues across restarts, and ScanImage's own stem, counter and frames-per-file settings are restored afterwards.
  • A short software-triggered recording has the requested frames and original pixel values, including a two-channel recording and a file rollover.
  • External triggering, first-frame timeout and abort behave as expected.
  • An automatic routine block arms ScanImage, the sequence's TTL starts the recording, and the response window lines up with the delivered pulse.
  • ScanImage runs as fast with NeuroSeq connected as without: compare its frame rate and dropped frames during Focus and a recording. Each status reply reports elapsed_ms, the time the call spent in ScanImage's MATLAB thread; NeuroSeq polls status five times a second. (The removed live view base64-encoded every frame in MATLAB, about 160 ms per 512×512 frame on that same thread, which is what slowed ScanImage down.)
  • Completed and interrupted recordings survive project save/reopen, and a recording finishing after a project switch attaches to its originating project.
  • Hardware stimulation markers and image timestamps agree before claiming any synchronization accuracy.

items.title: Future remote transport
items.text:
ScanImageConnection exchanges request IDs and JSON operations with a separate helper process. Commands, lifecycle status and recording indexes are independent of Qt rendering. A future remote transport can implement the same operations on the acquisition PC, with authentication, bounded messages, connection-loss reconciliation, and explicit recording transfer/path mapping. MATLAB Engine itself is used only locally. The current implementation opens no network server and relies on local filesystem access for recording verification.

Do not assume the built-in ScanImage TCP server speaks this protocol: its 2023 documentation describes a MATLAB client. Native ZeroMQ streaming requires ScanImage Premium 2025 or later and is not used here.

items.title: Adapter regression tests without a microscope
items.text:
In a separate MATLAB session with no hSI variable, from the repository root:

results = runtests('tests/matlab');
assertSuccess(results);

These tests use simulated ScanImage components to exercise settings restoration, callback registration, single-acquisition validation, and file naming. They do not establish compatibility with the installed ScanImage version or hardware timing.

items.title: Simulations
items.text: NeuroSeq runs Brian2 spiking network simulations. The model, parameters, stim arrays, and recorded monitors all live inside the project and are persisted together in the .nseq archive.

items.title: Running a simulation
items.text:
• Simulate → Run simulation (Ctrl+R) advances the network by the chosen duration. The run picks up from the last simulated time, so consecutive invocations extend the same trial.
  • If the project has an external simulator connected (see Run External Simulators), the action dispatches to that backend instead of the built-in Brian2 model.

items.title: Checkpointing
items.text:
Long simulations can be checkpointed so you can experiment from a known state without rerunning from scratch.

  • Simulate → Store simulation checkpoint (Ctrl+Shift+S) saves the current Brian2 network state (neuron variables, synapse weights, clock).
  • Simulate → Restore simulation checkpoint (Ctrl+Shift+R) rolls the network back to the most recently stored checkpoint. Trace, spike, and synapse monitors are truncated accordingly.

Checkpoints are part of the project file, so they survive save/load.

items.title: Choosing a Brian2 backend
items.text:
Settings → Brian2 simulation backend opens a small dialog to pick the Brian2 code-generation target:

  • cython — compiles C extensions on the fly. Fastest option for most networks; requires a working C toolchain (see the installation page for the MSVC note on Windows).
  • numpy — pure-Python fallback. Always works, slower. Tests use this.

items.title: Stimulation editor
items.text: The stim editor is the left-hand pane and operates in either draw or select mode, switched from the top of its toolbar. The general workflow is covered in GUI Overview → Stimulation editor; this section documents the editor's auxiliary tools.

items.title: Managing stim arrays
items.text:
The toolbar exposes three array-level actions:

  • Create stim array — opens a properties dialog: name, type (light, current, voltage, opsin, …), neuron count, physical units, and dt. The default dt is taken from Settings → Stimulus automatic padding (see below).
  • Edit stim array — change any of the above on the currently selected array. Editing the neuron count or dt resizes/resamples the existing data.
  • Delete stim array — drops the selected array from the project.

items.title: Reshaping the time axis
items.text:
• Pad stim array — extend the array's duration. You choose how much time to add and whether to pad at the start, end, or both. New samples are filled with zeros.
  • Trim stim array — shrink the array's duration. Useful after a simulation to discard the unused tail.
  • Clear stim array — zero every sample of the selected array without changing its shape.

items.title: Selection-mode operations
items.text:
When the editor is in select mode, mouse drags pick a rectangular region of the stim array. The toolbar then exposes:

  • Select all — extend the selection to the whole array.
  • Copy / Cut — copy or move the selected region to the internal clipboard.
  • Paste / Paste inverted — paste the clipboard at the current cursor position. Inverted swaps zero and non-zero samples on the way in (useful for stamping refractory windows between pulse trains).
  • Save selection to file / Load selection from file — read or write the selected region as a NumPy .npy blob. Loaded selections are inserted at the current cursor and respect the array's neuron axis.

Both modes share Undo / Redo at the top of the toolbar.

items.title: Toggling the grid
items.text: View → Toggle Grid turns the time and neuron grid overlays on or off in the stim editor. The grid spacing is fixed to the array's dt so it doubles as a sample ruler.

items.title: Pre-built stimulation patterns
items.text:
For common stimulation motifs you do not need to draw manually. The toolbar action Design static input opens a generator dialog that writes patterns directly into the selected stim array:

The same patterns, with the same names, are offered for All neurons and for Specific neurons; Für Elise, which plays fixed neurons, is for all neurons only.

Pattern Description Sequential One neuron after another, each firing Pulses per neuron pulses before the next Simultaneous All neurons of the scope fire together, with the same magnitude every pulse Linear gradient Like Simultaneous, but the magnitude steps linearly from the first to the last pulse Ramp A continuous linear ramp of the magnitude, repeated Für Elise The opening notes of Für Elise on neurons 0-5, with Pulses per note

Common controls:

  • Scope — apply to all neurons or to specific neuron indices.
  • Pulse duration / Inter-pulse interval (or Ramp duration / Interval between ramps) — in milliseconds.
  • Magnitude, or First / Last pulse magnitude for Linear gradient and Start / End magnitude for Ramp.
  • Sequence repetitions, Number of pulses, Number of ramps or Melody repetitions — how often the pattern repeats, named for the pattern.
  • Start time — where in the array the pattern begins.

The dialog stays open so you can iterate: change parameters, click Apply to overwrite, or Reset start time to rewind the cursor.

items.title: Closed-loop input design
items.text: Design dynamic input is a separate NeuroSeq feature for routines that extend a stim array, run a simulation, analyze its traces, and decide what to append next. Its first routine uses five-pulse EPSP measurements and STDP pairings to move a postsynaptic response toward a percentage target. See the dedicated Design dynamic input guide for setup, controls, the decision algorithm, live plots, and current limitations.

items.title: Looping a stim array
items.text: Loop stim array (toolbar) repeats the entire current array end-to-end a chosen number of times. The dialog lets you pick the number of repetitions; the loop runs in place — the array is extended to accommodate the repeats.

items.title: Settings that affect simulations
items.text:
• Settings → Stimulus automatic padding — default duration (in seconds) used when a new stim array is created and when Pad stim array prefills its dialog.
  • Settings → Brian2 simulation backend — described above.
  • Settings → Synapse matrix RAM limit — see GUI Overview → Synaptic data widget.

items.title: Editing the model
items.text: File → Edit model (Ctrl+E) opens the parameter tree editor for the underlying Brian2 model: neuron equations, parameter values, synapse rules, monitors. Changes take effect on the next Run simulation and are saved with the project.

items.title: Connecting simulations and experiments
items.text: A NeuroSeq project holds both simulated and recorded data side by side. Stim arrays drive simulations and document what was applied to a real sample, so the same draw-and-edit workflow works for both. This page covers the actions that move data between projects and between simulations and experiments.

items.title: Project as a container
items.text:
A project owns:

  • one or more stim arrays (Project.stim_arrays),
  • one Brian2 model (Project.b2_model),
  • a set of experiments (Project.experiments), each grouping TraceData, SpikeData, and SynapseData from a single run or recording,
  • optional Cellpose segmentation for hardware mapping.

Both the Run simulation action and the Run external stimulation function action produce a new experiment that is appended to this container.

items.title: Importing from another project
items.text:
File → Import from project merges data from an existing .nseq file into the current project. This is the right action when you want to:

  • pull in stim arrays designed in another project,
  • attach experimental traces or spikes recorded under a different model,
  • reuse a Cellpose segmentation across projects sharing the same microscope sample.

After picking the file, NeuroSeq shows the items it can pull in (stim arrays, experiments, segmentation) so you can opt in selectively. The current project's own data is left untouched.

items.title: Manage Data
items.text:
File → Manage Data opens the data manager dialog, which lists project data grouped by simulation run or recording. Each group corresponds to an Experiment in Project.experiments. From here you can:

  • inspect each group's name, duration, and number of datasets,
  • inspect which data objects (TraceData, SpikeData, SynapseData) belong to each group and their dimensions,
  • delete selected groups and all the datasets they contain.

items.title: Comparing simulated and recorded data
items.text:
The widgets (trace, spike, synapse, custom analysis) all draw from the project as a whole, so simulated and imported data can be displayed together:

  1. Run a simulation, or load a previously simulated experiment.
  2. Import experimental traces via Importing imaging data or Importing Igor2 waves.
  3. In the Neuron data dropdown, switch between the simulated and the imported TraceData — they share the same time axis whenever both were aligned to the same stim array.
  4. Use the All data ("Data") widget to display two TraceData objects in the same view for direct comparison.

The Analysis Tools and Custom Plugins page covers the right-click analyses that operate on a selected region of any widget — these work identically on simulated and recorded data, which is the point of keeping both in one container.

items.title: STDP synaptic tuning
items.text:
Design dynamic input is a closed-loop stimulation feature in NeuroSeq. Unlike Design static input, which writes a complete pattern before a simulation, Design dynamic input repeatedly performs three operations:

  1. append stimulation to the selected stim array,
  2. continue the Brian2 simulation, and
  3. analyze the resulting voltage trace to decide what to append next.

This guide covers STDP synaptic tuning, a routine that targets a postsynaptic EPSP amplitude by applying spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) pairings. The decision policy and protocol described below target this specific use case.

items.title: Opening Design dynamic input
items.text:
Select the stim array that should receive the generated protocol, then click Design dynamic input in the stimulation-editor toolbar. A prompt asks which design routine to run; choose STDP synaptic tuning to open the designer. The selected array must have columns for both the pre- and postsynaptic neuron IDs.

For a ready-to-run model, open:

File → Open example project → Network → Two Hodgkin-Huxley Neurons with STDP

In that example, use:

  • stim array: Exc_stimulation,
  • trace: Simulation :: P / v,
  • presynaptic neuron ID: 0, and
  • postsynaptic neuron ID: 1.

STDP synaptic tuning appends data; it does not clear an existing stim array. New blocks are placed after both the current array end and the current simulation time, so generated stimulation is never inserted into the already simulated past.

items.title: Closed-loop routine
items.text:
When Start routine is pressed, STDP synaptic tuning performs the following sequence:

  1. Append five probe pulses (default 1 ms each) for the presynaptic neuron. Probe pulses are spaced 100 ms apart.
  2. Continue the simulation through the appended block.
  3. Detect and average the five EPSP amplitudes in the postsynaptic voltage trace. This first average is the baseline and is defined as 100%.
  4. Compare the current percentage with Target relative EPSP amplitude.

  5. Append and simulate one plasticity-induction pairing. The selected pairing strategy determines the pulse order and timing.

  6. Append and simulate another five-pulse presynaptic probe block.

  7. Measure the new five-EPSP average and repeat from step 4 until the target is reached or the maximum number of induction pairings is exhausted.

The target is achieved when:

abs(current EPSP % - target EPSP %) < tolerance %

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Meaning Default Trace to analyze Simulation voltage trace containing the postsynaptic neuron First available trace Presynaptic neuron ID Stim-array column receiving probe pulses and the presynaptic side of a pairing 0 Postsynaptic neuron ID Trace index used for EPSP measurement and the postsynaptic side of a pairing 1 Pulse amplitude Value written into the selected stim array during each pulse 1.0 in array units Pulse duration (ms) Width of every probe and pairing pulse 1 ms Pairing strategy Fixed timing with automatic direction, or adaptive signed timing Fixed pre-post pairing time Pre-post pairing time Fixed-strategy interval; pulse order is selected automatically 30 ms Initial guess for pre-post pairing time Adaptive-strategy starting magnitude 30 ms dt increment Adaptive-strategy change applied to the signed pairing time each iteration 1 ms Target relative EPSP amplitude Desired EPSP relative to the first five-pulse baseline 120% Tolerance window (deadband) Maximum absolute distance from the target that counts as success 1% Maximum plasticity induction iterations Safety limit for closed-loop iterations 20 Run until the last iteration regardless of convergence to the target Ignore early convergence and continue until the maximum pairing count Disabled Follow new input on each iteration Move the synchronized timeline camera to each appended block Enabled Visible history Number of generated-block lengths kept visible throughout execution 3

Set Visible history to 0 to show only the newly appended block. Disable Follow new input on each iteration to retain manual control of the shared pan and zoom state.

Normally, entering the tolerance stops the routine immediately. Enable Run until the last iteration regardless of convergence to the target to keep applying induction pairings until Maximum plasticity induction iterations is reached. Convergence is still measured and recorded in the log while this override is active.

items.title: Pairing strategies
items.text:
Fixed pre-post pairing time keeps the configured interval magnitude constant. Below the EPSP target it uses pre-before-post timing; above the target it uses post-before-pre timing.

Adaptive (single parameter, dt increment) starts with the initial pairing time magnitude. After each new EPSP measurement, it compares the remaining target error with the change since the preceding measurement. If abs(EPSP new - target) > abs(EPSP new - EPSP old), the magnitude is reduced by dt increment (not below zero); otherwise it is increased by dt increment. The current target side determines the sign: positive/pre-before- post below target and negative/post-before-pre above target.

items.title: EPSP measurement
items.text:
STDP synaptic tuning reuses NeuroSeq's existing EPSP amplitudes analysis plugin. The plugin:

  • converts supported voltage units to millivolts,
  • detects peaks using an adaptive prominence threshold,
  • measures amplitude relative to a local pre-peak baseline, and
  • rejects action-potential-sized peaks.

STDP synaptic tuning associates detections with the five known probe times and uses their mean as the current EPSP amplitude. If the selected trace does not record the postsynaptic neuron, or if an EPSP cannot be detected after every probe, the routine stops and reports the reason in its log.

items.title: Creating simulation trace monitors
items.text:
A freshly loaded model may not expose its simulation trace names until Brian2 has initialized the network. If no trace is available when the routine starts, STDP synaptic tuning opens Create stimulation trace monitor and offers to run a short initialization simulation.

  • default duration: 0.001 s,
  • precision: three decimal places,
  • minimum duration: 0.001 s.

After the initialization run, STDP synaptic tuning refreshes the trace list and starts the EPSP routine automatically. If no trace becomes available, add a Brian2 StateMonitor for the membrane-voltage variable in File → Edit model, then try again.

items.title: Live plots
items.text:
The dialog contains three synchronized Matplotlib plots with enough spacing to keep their labels and tick marks separate:

  • EPSP amplitude (%) shows every five-pulse measurement relative to the initial baseline. The target appears as a dashed horizontal line after the baseline has been measured. The shaded region is the tolerance deadband.
  • Δ target (%) shows the signed difference between the current EPSP and the target. Zero means that the measured value equals the target; the shaded band shows the same tolerance around zero.
  • Pairing time (ms) shows the signed pre-post pairing time used for each induction. Positive points are pre-before-post and negative points are post-before-pre.

The text below the plots reports the signed difference, absolute difference, and active tolerance. Plot colors follow NeuroSeq's light or dark theme.

items.title: Stopping and reviewing the result
items.text:
Stop prevents the routine from appending another block after the current simulation finishes. It does not cancel a Brian2 task already in progress; use the simulation progress dialog's cancellation control when the active run must be interrupted.

All generated blocks remain in the selected stim array and can be inspected, edited, undone, saved with the project, or used for subsequent simulations. The routine log records baseline measurements, relative changes, induction direction, termination, and errors.

items.title: Current limitations
items.text:
• The routine currently supports the built-in Brian2 simulation path.
  • The decision policy assumes excitatory EPSPs and an STDP model in which pre-before-post potentiates and post-before-pre depresses.
  • Probe timing is fixed to five pulses (of configurable duration) at 100 ms intervals.
  • Only one selected stim array is modified, although NeuroSeq pads other arrays as needed to maintain a compatible project timeline.
  • EPSP detection requires a voltage TraceData object and a detectable response after each probe pulse.
